None of the five jumps is significant. The margin of the previous election jumps by 0.7 points, with an interval from -7.0 to 10.9: not zero for certain, but no pattern either.

Placebo cutoffs and the donut

At other values of the margin nobody wins or loses anything, so there should be no jump. And the result should not depend on the few elections right at the edge:

Code 
cuts <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(-20, -15, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 15, 20), function(k) {
    zz <- if (k < 0) {
      subset(s, margin < 0)
    } else if (k > 0) {
      subset(s, margin >= 0)
    } else {
      s
    }
    m <- rdrobust(zz$vote, zz$margin, c = k)
    data.frame(
      cutoff = k,
      jump = m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      low = m$ci["Robust", 1],
      high = m$ci["Robust", 2],
      p = m$pv["Robust", 1],
      n = sum(m$N_h)
    )
  })
)
print(round(cuts, 3), row.names = FALSE)
 cutoff    jump     low   high     p   n
    -20   6.620  -3.017 17.845 0.164 142
    -15  -6.893 -19.112  4.660 0.233 144
    -10 -23.216 -42.861 -7.857 0.005  59
     -5  -0.177 -12.809  8.871 0.722 210
      0   7.414   4.094 10.919 0.000 683
      5   3.321  -4.719  7.311 0.673 238
     10   2.915  -1.087 11.037 0.108 145
     15  -1.218 -13.861  8.620 0.648 110
     20  -0.250 -12.847 14.721 0.894 111
Code 
donut <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2), function(k) {
    zz <- subset(s, abs(margin) >= k)
    m <- rdrobust(zz$vote, zz$margin)
    data.frame(
      left_out_within = k,
      removed = nrow(s) - nrow(zz),
      jump = m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      low = m$ci["Robust", 1],
      high = m$ci["Robust", 2]
    )
  })
)
print(round(donut, 2), row.names = FALSE)
 left_out_within removed jump  low  high
            0.00       0 7.41 4.09 10.92
            0.25       9 6.94 3.31 10.45
            0.50      23 7.09 3.20 10.83
            1.00      43 6.58 2.19 10.60
            2.00      96 4.70 0.21  8.95
Code 
ggplot(cuts, aes(cutoff, jump)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high, colour = cutoff == 0), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = cutoff == 0), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cuts$cutoff) +
  labs(
    title = "The jump at the real cutoff (orange) and at eight false ones",
    subtitle = "Robust 95% intervals",
    x = "cutoff (points of margin)",
    y = "jump"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
false_cuts <- subset(cuts, cutoff != 0); odd <- subset(false_cuts, p < .05)

Of the eight false cutoffs, 1 has p < .05: at -10 a “jump” of -23.2 points, from 59 elections. Among eight tests that happens by chance in about a third of the cases (\(1 - 0.95^8\) = 0.34), and here the interval is very wide. We report it all the same. Without the elections within 0.5 points (23 of them) the effect is 7.1, without those within 1 point 6.6; without those within 2 points it is 4.7, and the interval begins near zero.

6. What not to do: a global polynomial

Before local regression became common, people fitted a high polynomial in the running variable to all data and read off the jump:

Code 
global <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(1:6, function(p) {
    m <- lm(vote ~ won * poly(margin, p, raw = TRUE), s)
    data.frame(
      degree = p,
      jump = coef(m)[["won"]],
      SE = sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = "HC1")["won", "won"])
    )
  })
)
print(round(global, 2), row.names = FALSE)
 degree jump   SE
      1 6.04 0.89
      2 4.93 1.13
      3 7.32 1.40
      4 9.41 1.66
      5 7.96 1.97
      6 6.63 2.29

The answer goes from 4.9 to 9.4 with the degree, and each has a small standard error that knows nothing of the choice. A polynomial lets elections that were won by 80 points have a say about the edge (Gelman & Imbens, 2019). Local lines do not.

7. Are the intervals right? A simulation

We make a population that looks like ours: the curve is a polynomial of degree 4 on each side (so the true jump is known), the margins come from the data, the noise is normal. Draw 500 samples and let rdrobust() do everything, bandwidth included.

Code 
sim_rd <- function(degree, reps = 500) {
  ml <- lm(vote ~ poly(margin, degree, raw = TRUE), s, subset = won == 0)
  mr <- lm(vote ~ poly(margin, degree, raw = TRUE), s, subset = won == 1)
  mu <- ifelse(s$won == 1, predict(mr, s), predict(ml, s))
  truth <- coef(mr)[[1]] - coef(ml)[[1]]
  sigma <- sd(s$vote - mu)
  r <- replicate(reps, {
    i <- sample(nrow(s), replace = TRUE)
    m <- rdrobust(mu[i] + rnorm(nrow(s), 0, sigma), s$margin[i], masspoints = "off")
    c(
      m$coef["Conventional", 1],
      m$ci["Conventional", 1] < truth & truth < m$ci["Conventional", 2],
      m$ci["Robust", 1] < truth & truth < m$ci["Robust", 2],
      m$bws["h", "left"]
    )
  })
  data.frame(
    degree = degree,
    true_jump = truth,
    mean_estimate = mean(r[1, ]),
    mean_bandwidth = mean(r[4, ]),
    coverage_usual = mean(r[2, ]),
    coverage_robust = mean(r[3, ])
  )
}
set.seed(221); sims <- do.call(rbind, lapply(3:5, sim_rd))
print(round(sims, 3), row.names = FALSE)
 degree true_jump mean_estimate mean_bandwidth coverage_usual coverage_robust
      3     7.319         7.052         19.631          0.952           0.960
      4     9.407         8.735         16.498          0.910           0.950
      5     7.958         7.950         17.866          0.948           0.948

The usual interval contains the truth in 91.0% to 95.2% of the samples, depending on how much the curve bends at the edge. The robust interval has 94.8% to 96.0%. Where the true curve bends strongly at the edge, the local linear estimate is too low on average (degree 4: 8.7 instead of 9.4), and the robust interval is what saves us.

8. What the number means

  • It is the effect at the cutoff, for elections that were nearly tied. A safe seat may be different.
  • It is the advantage of the party that holds the seat, not of the person: the candidate in the next election may be a new one.
  • What about winning again? The same design with the outcome “the Democrat gets more than half of the votes next time”:
Code 
s$wins_next <- as.numeric(s$vote > 50)
win <- rdrobust(s$wins_next, s$margin); clustered <- rdrobust(s$vote, s$margin, cluster = s$state)
c(
  jump_in_the_probability_to_win = win$coef["Conventional", 1],
  low = win$ci["Robust", 1],
  high = win$ci["Robust", 2]
)
jump_in_the_probability_to_win                            low                           high 
                     0.3301591                      0.1847127                      0.4604589
Code 
cbind(
  value = c(
    effect_on_the_share_clustered_by_state = clustered$coef["Conventional", 1],
    low = clustered$ci["Robust", 1],
    high = clustered$ci["Robust", 2]
  )
)
                                           value
effect_on_the_share_clustered_by_state  7.394838
low                                     3.984970
high                                   11.024943

A narrow win raises the probability of a majority next time by 33.0 percentage points, 95% CI [18.5, 46.0]. (With more than two candidates more than half is stricter than winning.) With standard errors clustered by state, the interval for the share is [4.0, 11.0]: no important change.

9. Things to keep in mind

  • Draw the plot first. If you cannot see the jump, be careful with the number.
  • Know the rule. Is the threshold applied strictly? Do other things change at the same threshold (another law at age 18)? Then the jump is the effect of all of them.
  • Fuzzy RD: when crossing the threshold only raises the probability of treatment, divide the jump in the outcome by the jump in the treatment. That is instrumental variables at the cutoff: rdrobust(y, x, fuzzy = treatment).
  • Discrete running variables (age in years, whole test points): there is no “just above”; the methods need care.
  • Control variables are not needed. They can shorten the interval (covs =), and must be fixed before the treatment.
  • Report the bandwidth, its selection, the kernel, the number of observations on each side within it, and the robust interval. Show other bandwidths.
  • Power is low: only the observations near the edge count. Here 683 of 1,297.

10. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the rule and the running variable, the cutoff, the estimator (degree, kernel, bandwidth and how it was chosen), the numbers of observations on each side within the bandwidth, the estimate with a robust interval, and the checks. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
line <- function(label, m, scale = 1) {
  data.frame(
    Outcome = label,
    n = paste(m$N_h, collapse = " / "),
    h = f1(m$bws["h", "left"]),
    jump = f2(scale * m$coef["Conventional", 1]),
    ci = paste0("[", f2(scale * m$ci["Robust", 1]), ", ", f2(scale * m$ci["Robust", 2]), "]"),
    p = sub("= ", "", pval(m$pv["Robust", 1]))
  )
}
pm <- function(v) rdrobust(sorted[[v]], sorted$margin)
apa_table <- rbind(
  line("Share in the next election (%)", fit_rd),
  line("Majority in the next election (percentage points)", win, 100),
  line("Margin of the previous election (placebo)", pm("previous_margin")),
  line("Earlier terms in the House (placebo)", pm("termshouse")),
  line("Earlier terms in the Senate (placebo)", pm("termssenate")),
  line("Log population (placebo)", pm("log_population"))
)

Method (data analysis):

The effect of holding a US Senate seat on the party’s share in the next election was estimated with a sharp regression discontinuity design (Lee, 2008), using 1,297 elections between 1914 and 2004 (Cattaneo et al., 2015). The running variable was the Democratic margin of victory, with a cutoff of zero. We fitted local linear regressions with a triangular kernel on each side of the cutoff, with the bandwidth that minimises the mean squared error, and report robust bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals (Calonico et al., 2014; R package rdrobust). The assumption that parties could not steer the margin was examined with the density test of Cattaneo et al. (2020), and the continuity assumption with predetermined outcomes, false cutoffs, and the removal of the elections nearest the cutoff. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

A narrow win raised the party’s share in the next election by 7.4 percentage points, robust 95% CI [4.1, 10.9], p < .001 (bandwidth 17.8 points; 360 elections below and 323 above the cutoff; Table 1), and the probability of a majority by 33.0 percentage points, 95% CI [18.5, 46.0]. There was no evidence of a discontinuity in the density of the margin (T = -0.76, p = .447) or in the predetermined variables (p ≥ .498). Of eight false cutoffs, 1 showed a jump with p < .05. Estimates for bandwidths between 10 and 60 points ranged from 6.1 to 8.0.

Table 1

Discontinuities at a Margin of Zero

Outcome n below / above Bandwidth Jump Robust 95% CI p
Share in the next election (%) 360 / 323 17.8 7.41 [4.09, 10.92] < .001
Majority in the next election (percentage points) 467 / 439 28.4 33.02 [18.47, 46.05] < .001
Margin of the previous election (placebo) 298 / 279 17.8 0.71 [-7.05, 10.91] .674
Earlier terms in the House (placebo) 282 / 257 15.7 -0.17 [-1.27, 0.69] .561
Earlier terms in the Senate (placebo) 291 / 267 16.4 -0.19 [-1.56, 1.37] .900
Log population (placebo) 392 / 355 18.5 -0.11 [-0.52, 0.29] .581

Note. Local linear regression, triangular kernel, bandwidth chosen to minimise the mean squared error separately for each outcome. n: elections within the bandwidth.

Points to remember:

  • Report the estimate of the local linear fit and the robust interval.
  • Give the bandwidth, and the number of observations on each side of it.
  • Show the plot, the density test and the placebo outcomes.
  • Say that the effect is for the units at the cutoff.

11. Summary

When A treatment is given by a threshold in a running variable that nobody controls exactly
The effect The jump of the regression function at the cutoff
Estimator Weighted lines on each side, within a bandwidth: lm(y ~ D * x, weights = triangle)
Bandwidth Minimises the mean squared error (rdrobust)
Interval Robust bias-corrected (with the same bandwidth for the bias: the local quadratic fit)
How (R) rdrobust(y, x, c = 0), rddensity(x), rdplot(y, x)
Checks Density, placebo outcomes, false cutoffs, donut, other bandwidths
Not Global polynomials
Related pages Instrumental variables, LOESS, simple regression

References

Calonico, S., Cattaneo, M. D., & Titiunik, R. (2014). Robust nonparametric confidence intervals for regression-discontinuity designs. Econometrica, 82(6), 2295–2326. https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA11757

Cattaneo, M. D., Frandsen, B. R., & Titiunik, R. (2015). Randomization inference in the regression discontinuity design: An application to party advantages in the U.S. Senate. Journal of Causal Inference, 3(1), 1–24. https://doi.org/10.1515/jci-2013-0010

Cattaneo, M. D., Jansson, M., & Ma, X. (2020). Simple local polynomial density estimators. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 115(531), 1449–1455. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2019.1635480

Gelman, A., & Imbens, G. (2019). Why high-order polynomials should not be used in regression discontinuity designs. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 37(3), 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1080/07350015.2017.1366909

Lee, D. S. (2008). Randomized experiments from non-random selection in U.S. House elections. Journal of Econometrics, 142(2), 675–697. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.004

McCrary, J. (2008). Manipulation of the running variable in the regression discontinuity design: A density test. Journal of Econometrics, 142(2), 698–714. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.005

Thistlethwaite, D. L., & Campbell, D. T. (1960). Regression-discontinuity analysis: An alternative to the ex post facto experiment. Journal of Educational Psychology, 51(6), 309–317. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0044319

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Instrumental Variables: What Is a Year of School Worth?
item.description: Instrumental variables and two-stage least squares in R with ivreg, on Card’s 3,010 young men and the college near home: why least squares is wrong when something unseen matters, the conditions for an instrument, the Wald estimator and two-stage least squares by hand, why the second stage gives wrong standard errors, the first-stage F, Wu-Hausman and Sargan tests by hand, weak instruments in a simulation and the Anderson-Rubin interval, whose effect it is, how small a violation would change the answer, a control that is not innocent, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Instrumental variables and two-stage least squares in R with ivreg, on Card’s 3,010 young men and the college near home: why least squares is wrong when something unseen matters, the conditions for an instrument, the Wald estimator and two-stage least squares by hand, why the second stage gives wrong standard errors, the first-stage F, Wu-Hausman and Sargan tests by hand, weak instruments in a simulation and the Anderson-Rubin interval, whose effect it is, how small a violation would change the answer, a control that is not innocent, and APA reporting.

The question: school, or what comes with it?

People with more schooling earn more. Is it the school that makes the difference? Or would the same persons have earned more anyway, because they are able, hard-working, or from families that help? Nobody can measure all of that. So adding control variables, the remedy of ordinary regression, does not finish the job.

An instrumental variable (an instrument) takes another way. Find something that

  • pushes people towards more schooling,
  • has nothing to do with their ability or family,
  • and touches their wages in no other way than through schooling.

Then compare the wages of those who were pushed and those who were not. Whatever difference there is, must have come through schooling.

David Card (1993) proposed the distance to a college. A boy who grew up near a four-year college could live at home while studying. For some boys that decided the matter. This page repeats his analysis, with every step by hand, and then asks how far one can trust it. The second part is the more important one: the conditions above cannot be proved from the data.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(ivreg)       # ivreg(): two-stage least squares with diagnostics
# also used, with package::function: sandwich (robust standard errors)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# APA: no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0\\.", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
}
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

1. The data

Code 
card <- read.csv("https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/wooldridge/card.csv")
dim(card)
[1] 3010   35
Code 
head(
  card[, c(
    "lwage", "wage", "educ", "age", "exper", "black", "south", "smsa", "smsa66", "nearc4", "nearc2"
  )],
  4
)
     lwage wage educ age exper black south smsa smsa66 nearc4 nearc2
1 6.306275  548    7  29    16     1     0    1      1      0      0
2 6.175867  481   12  27     9     0     0    1      1      0      0
3 6.580639  721   12  34    16     0     0    1      1      0      0
4 5.521461  250   11  27    10     0     0    1      1      1      1
Code 
controls <- paste(
  "exper + expersq + black + south + smsa + smsa66",
  "+ reg662 + reg663 + reg664 + reg665 + reg666 + reg667 + reg668 + reg669"
)

3,010 men of the US National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men, 24 to 34 years old when their wages were asked in 1976. The file comes from the R package wooldridge. The variables:

  • lwage: the logarithm of the hourly wage (in cents). A coefficient of 0.10 means about 10% more.
  • educ: years of schooling.
  • nearc4: 1 if there was an accredited four-year college in the local labour market, judged by the county where he lived in 1966 (as a boy or very young man), otherwise 0. nearc2 is the same for two-year colleges.
  • The controls of Card: years of potential work experience (exper, which is age − schooling − 6, and its square), black, living in the south, living in a metropolitan area in 1976 (smsa) and in 1966 (smsa66), and the region in 1966 (eight indicator variables, reg662 to reg669).

2. Look at the data

Code 
m_ed <- aggregate(lwage ~ educ, card, function(v) c(mean(v), length(v)))
m_ed <- data.frame(educ = m_ed$educ, lwage = m_ed$lwage[, 1], n = m_ed$lwage[, 2])
ggplot(subset(m_ed, n >= 10), aes(educ, lwage)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(
    data = card,
    aes(educ, lwage),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 8) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean log wage by years of schooling",
    subtitle = "Size of the points: number of men",
    x = "years of schooling",
    y = "mean log wage"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
by_near <- aggregate(cbind(educ, lwage, black, south, smsa66) ~ nearc4, card, mean)
by_near$n <- as.numeric(table(card$nearc4))
print(round(by_near, 3), row.names = FALSE)
 nearc4   educ lwage black south smsa66    n
      0 12.698 6.155 0.280 0.563  0.328  957
      1 13.527 6.311 0.212 0.329  0.799 2053

The men who grew up near a college (2,053 of them) have 0.83 years more schooling and wages that are 0.156 higher in logs. But they are also different in other ways: fewer are black, fewer live in the south, and most come from cities. A college does not stand just anywhere. So the instrument is at best clean after controlling for region and city.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: why least squares is wrong

The true equation has a variable \(u\) that we cannot see, which is also related to schooling \(s\):

\[\log w = \beta\, s + u, \qquad \text{Cov}(s, u) \ne 0\]

Least squares attributes to \(s\) everything that comes along with it, \(\hat\beta_{OLS} \to \beta + \text{Cov}(s, u)/\text{Var}(s)\). The sample size does not help.

Code 
nodes <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 2, 4, 3),
  y = c(0, 0, 0, 1.3),
  label = c(
    "college nearby\n(instrument)",
    "schooling",
    "wage",
    "ability, family, ...\n(not observed)"
  )
)
arrows <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.5, 2.4, 2.8, 3.2),
  y = c(0, 0, 1.05, 1.05),
  xend = c(1.55, 3.65, 2.15, 3.85),
  yend = c(0, 0, 0.15, 0.15)
)
never <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.3, 0.1),
  y = c(-0.15, 0.2),
  xend = c(3.8, 2.3),
  yend = c(-0.15, 1.2),
  curv = 1
)
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = arrows,
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "#2a78d6"
  ) +
  geom_curve(
    data = never[1, ],
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = 0.25,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = never[2, ],
    aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4.2, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2,
    y = -0.78,
    label = "no direct way (exclusion)",
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.75,
    y = 0.95,
    label = "no connection\n(independence)",
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  xlim(-0.6, 4.6) +
  ylim(-0.95, 1.6) +
  labs(title = "What an instrument needs: the blue arrows, and not the dashed lines") +
  theme_void()

Step 2: the conditions

  1. Relevance: the instrument changes schooling. This can be checked.
  2. Independence: the instrument has nothing to do with \(u\) (after the controls).
  3. Exclusion: the instrument changes wages only through schooling.
  4. Monotonicity (for the interpretation, section 6): the instrument pushes nobody in the opposite direction.

Step 3: the Wald estimator

With one instrument that is 0 or 1 and no controls, the estimator is the ratio of two differences:

\[\hat\beta_{IV} = \frac{\bar y_{\text{near}} - \bar y_{\text{far}}}{\bar s_{\text{near}} - \bar s_{\text{far}}}\]

The numerator is the effect of the instrument on the outcome (the reduced form), the denominator its effect on schooling (the first stage).

Code 
c(
  reduced_form = diff(by_near$lwage),
  first_stage = diff(by_near$educ),
  Wald = diff(by_near$lwage) / diff(by_near$educ)
)
reduced_form  first_stage         Wald 
   0.1559075    0.8290190    0.1880626

Without controls we know that condition 2 fails, so 0.188 is not our answer.

Step 4: two-stage least squares

With controls \(X\) (and perhaps several instruments \(Z\)) the same idea is done with two regressions, two-stage least squares (2SLS):

  1. First stage: regress schooling on the instrument and the controls, and keep the fitted values \(\hat s\). They contain only the part of schooling that the instrument and the controls can explain.
  2. Second stage: regress the log wage on \(\hat s\) and the controls.

\[\hat\beta = (W^\top P_Z W)^{-1} W^\top P_Z\, y, \qquad P_Z = Z(Z^\top Z)^{-1}Z^\top\]

(\(W\): schooling and the controls; \(Z\): instrument and controls.)

Code 
fml <- function(lhs, rhs) as.formula(paste(lhs, "~", rhs))
ols          <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls)), card)
first_stage  <- lm(fml("educ", paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
reduced_form <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
card$educ_hat <- fitted(first_stage)
second_stage <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ_hat +", controls)), card)
W <- model.matrix(ols); Z <- model.matrix(first_stage); y <- card$lwage
PW   <- Z %*% solve(crossprod(Z), crossprod(Z, W))                        # P_Z W
beta <- drop(solve(crossprod(PW, W), crossprod(PW, y)))
cbind(
  value = c(
    OLS = coef(ols)[["educ"]],
    reduced_form_over_first_stage = coef(reduced_form)[["nearc4"]] / coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]],
    second_stage = coef(second_stage)[["educ_hat"]],
    matrix_formula = beta[["educ"]]
  )
)
                                   value
OLS                           0.07469326
reduced_form_over_first_stage 0.13150384
second_stage                  0.13150384
matrix_formula                0.13150384

The three ways give the same 0.132. Least squares gave 0.075.

Step 5: the standard error

The second regression gives the right coefficient and a wrong standard error: its residuals are measured from \(\hat s\) instead of \(s\). The right ones use the real schooling:

\[e = y - W\hat\beta, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat\beta) = \frac{e^\top e}{n - p}\,(W^\top P_Z W)^{-1}\]

Code 
e  <- drop(y - W %*% beta); s2 <- sum(e^2) / (nrow(W) - ncol(W))
se <- sqrt(diag(s2 * solve(crossprod(PW))))
iv <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc4 +", controls)), data = card)
rbind(
  by_hand = c(estimate = beta[["educ"]], SE = se[["educ"]]),
  ivreg = coef(summary(iv))["educ", 1:2],
  second_stage_lm = coef(summary(second_stage))["educ_hat", 1:2]
)
                 estimate         SE
by_hand         0.1315038 0.05496367
ivreg           0.1315038 0.05496367
second_stage_lm 0.1315038 0.05651035
Code 
robust_se <- sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1")["educ", "educ"]); c(robust_SE = robust_se)
 robust_SE 
0.05414362

Here the wrong standard error happens to be close to the right one. It can be far off, in both directions. In ivreg(), the part after | lists the instruments and all controls again.

4. Reading the output

Code 
ci_iv <- confint(iv)["educ", ]; s_iv <- summary(iv)
round(
  rbind(
    OLS = c(coef(summary(ols))["educ", ], confint(ols)["educ", ]),
    IV = c(coef(s_iv)["educ", ], ci_iv)
  ),
  4
)
    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  2.5 % 97.5 %
OLS   0.0747     0.0035 21.3510   0.0000 0.0678 0.0816
IV    0.1315     0.0550  2.3926   0.0168 0.0237 0.2393
Code 
s_iv$diagnostics
                 df1  df2 statistic      p-value
Weak instruments   1 2994 13.255785 0.0002763401
Wu-Hausman         1 2993  1.167645 0.2799726211
Sargan             0   NA        NA           NA
  • The IV estimate says that a year of schooling raises the wage by 0.132 (about 14%), 95% CI [0.024, 0.239]. Least squares says 0.075 (7.8%).
  • The interval of IV is 15.7 times as wide. That is the price. IV uses only the little variation of schooling that comes from the instrument. With the partial correlation \(r\) between instrument and schooling, the SE grows by about \(1/|r|\); here \(r\) = 0.066.
  • The IV estimate is higher than that of least squares. If able men stay longer in school, we expected the opposite. Section 6 comes back to this.

The numbers are those of Card’s own Table 3: 0.320 (0.088) for the first stage, 0.042 (0.018) for the reduced form and 0.132 (0.055) for the IV estimate. The three tests of the output, by hand:

Code 
fs_without <- update(first_stage, . ~ . - nearc4)
# weak instruments: the F of the instrument in the first stage
F_first <- anova(fs_without, first_stage)[2, "F"]
card$v_hat <- residuals(first_stage)
# Wu-Hausman: the first-stage residual as an extra predictor
wu <- coef(summary(update(ols, . ~ . + v_hat)))["v_hat", ]
# two instruments
iv2 <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc2 + nearc4 +", controls)), data = card)
# Sargan: n R^2 of the IV residuals on all instruments
aux <- lm(fml("residuals(iv2)", paste("nearc2 + nearc4 +", controls)), card)
c(
  F_first_stage = F_first,
  F_Wu_Hausman = wu[["t value"]]^2,
  Sargan_two_instruments = nrow(card) * summary(aux)$r.squared
)
         F_first_stage           F_Wu_Hausman Sargan_two_instruments 
             13.255785               1.167645               1.248153
Code 
summary(iv2)$diagnostics; coef(summary(iv2))["educ", 1:2]
                 df1  df2 statistic      p-value
Weak instruments   2 2993  7.893096 0.0003811364
Wu-Hausman         1 2993  2.925645 0.0872860158
Sargan             1   NA  1.248153 0.2639054547
  Estimate Std. Error 
0.15705937 0.05257824
Code 
sargan <- summary(iv2)$diagnostics["Sargan", ]
weak2 <- summary(iv2)$diagnostics["Weak instruments", ]
  • Weak instruments: the F of the instrument in the first stage, here 13.3. More about it in section 5.
  • Wu–Hausman: is the IV estimate different from least squares? Put the first-stage residual into the wage equation; if it matters, schooling is endogenous. Here F = 1.17, p = .280: the data cannot tell the two apart. That does not prove that least squares is right; the IV estimate is just imprecise.
  • Sargan: with more instruments than needed one can check whether they tell the same story. With the two-year college as second instrument the estimate is 0.157 and the test has p = .264: no contradiction. But two instruments of the same kind can be wrong in the same way, and then the test does not notice. (The F for both together is 7.9: the second one adds almost nothing.)

5. Weak instruments

If the instrument hardly moves schooling, the estimator divides by a number near zero. The estimates jump around, and the usual interval (estimate ± 1.96 SE) can be wrong. A simulation where we know the truth (β = 0.08). pi is the effect of the instrument on schooling, rho the endogeneity: the correlation between what we do not see in schooling and what we do not see in wages.

Code 
set.seed(211)
one <- function(pi, rho, n = 1000) {
  z <- rep(0:1, length.out = n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  s <- 12 + pi * z + 2 * (rho * u + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n))
  y <- 0.08 * s + 0.4 * u
  zc <- z - mean(z)
  fs <- sum(zc * s) / sum(zc^2)
  rf <- sum(zc * y) / sum(zc^2)
  b <- rf / fs
  e <- (y - mean(y)) - b * (s - mean(s))
  se <- sqrt(sum(e^2) / (n - 2) / sum(zc^2)) / abs(fs)
  F <- fs^2 * sum(zc^2) / (sum(((s - mean(s)) - fs * zc)^2) / (n - 2))
  d <- (y - mean(y)) - 0.08 * (s - mean(s))
  g <- sum(zc * d) / sum(zc^2)
  ar <- g / sqrt(sum((d - g * zc)^2) / (n - 2) / sum(zc^2)) # Anderson-Rubin at the truth
  c(
    iv = b,
    ols = cov(s, y) / var(s),
    F = F,
    covered = abs(b - 0.08) < 1.96 * se,
    ar_covered = abs(ar) < 1.96
  )
}
settings <- expand.grid(pi = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1), rho = c(0.6, 0.95))
sim <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(settings)), function(i) {
    r <- t(replicate(2000, one(settings$pi[i], settings$rho[i])))
    data.frame(
      settings[i, ],
      mean_F = mean(r[, "F"]),
      OLS = mean(r[, "ols"]),
      IV_median = median(r[, "iv"]),
      IV_low = quantile(r[, "iv"], 0.05),
      IV_high = quantile(r[, "iv"], 0.95),
      coverage = mean(r[, "covered"]),
      coverage_AR = mean(r[, "ar_covered"])
    )
  })
)
print(round(sim, 3), row.names = FALSE)
   pi  rho mean_F   OLS IV_median IV_low IV_high coverage coverage_AR
 0.10 0.60  1.760 0.200     0.147 -0.820   0.911    0.954       0.946
 0.25 0.60  4.963 0.200     0.084 -0.323   0.232    0.942       0.944
 0.50 0.60 16.762 0.198     0.082 -0.040   0.150    0.948       0.954
 1.00 0.60 63.829 0.193     0.081  0.031   0.118    0.954       0.951
 0.10 0.95  1.649 0.270     0.163 -0.616   0.994    0.791       0.954
 0.25 0.95  4.984 0.269     0.083 -0.465   0.183    0.890       0.954
 0.50 0.95 16.229 0.267     0.078 -0.061   0.138    0.938       0.948
 1.00 0.95 63.174 0.259     0.079  0.027   0.114    0.955       0.954
Code 
si <- function(p, r) sim[sim$pi == p & sim$rho == r, ]
c(endogeneity_in_the_data_of_Card = cor(residuals(iv), residuals(first_stage)))
endogeneity_in_the_data_of_Card 
                     -0.2851473
  • Least squares gives about 0.20 with an endogeneity of 0.6 and 0.27 with 0.95, instead of 0.08, whatever the instrument.
  • With a strong instrument (mean F = 63.8) the IV estimates lie around 0.08.
  • With the weakest one (mean F = 1.8) the median of the IV estimates is 0.15 or 0.16: it has moved towards least squares. And 90% of the estimates lie between -0.82 and 0.91 (endogeneity 0.6).
  • The usual interval contains the truth in 94% to 95% of the samples with an endogeneity of 0.6, even with weak instruments. It is right there, and very wide. With 0.95 its coverage falls to 79% for the weakest instrument.

This is why the advice in the literature looks contradictory. An old rule asks for F > 10 (Staiger & Stock, 1997). Lee et al. (2022) show that a t test with the usual 1.96 needs an F above 104.7 to have an error of at most 5% in the worst case. Angrist and Kolesár (2024) show that with one instrument the usual interval is nearly right unless the endogeneity is extreme. Card’s instrument has an F of 13.3, and the estimated endogeneity is -0.29. It is best to use an interval that does not depend on all this:

The Anderson–Rubin interval

A test that works with any strength (Anderson & Rubin, 1949): if the true effect were \(\beta_0\), then \(y - \beta_0 s\) would contain nothing of schooling, and the instrument should not predict it. Test that for many \(\beta_0\) and keep those that are not rejected. In the simulation it has the right coverage in all settings (from 94.3% to 95.4%).

Code 
ar_p <- function(b0) {
  r <- lm(fml(paste0("I(lwage - ", b0, " * educ)"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card)
  coef(summary(r))["nearc4", 4]
}
grid  <- seq(-0.05, 0.4, by = 0.005); p_grid <- sapply(grid, ar_p)
edge  <- function(a, b) uniroot(function(v) ar_p(v) - 0.05, c(a, b))$root
ci_ar <- c(edge(-0.05, beta[["educ"]]), edge(beta[["educ"]], 0.5))
rbind(Wald = ci_iv, Anderson_Rubin = ci_ar)
                    2.5 %    97.5 %
Wald           0.02373345 0.2392742
Anderson_Rubin 0.02480370 0.2848301
Code 
ggplot(data.frame(grid, p_grid), aes(grid, p_grid)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(ols)[["educ"]], colour = "#eb6834") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = coef(ols)[["educ"]] - 0.005,
    y = 0.95,
    label = "least squares",
    hjust = 1,
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Anderson-Rubin: p-value of every possible effect",
    subtitle = "Values above the dashed line (.05) form the 95% interval",
    x = "effect of a year of schooling on the log wage",
    y = "p"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

The interval goes from 0.025 to 0.285. It is longer than the usual one on the upper side, and it contains the result of least squares.

6. Whose effect is it?

Card’s result (IV higher than OLS) is typical for this literature. One explanation is that the effect is not the same for everybody. Boys who would go to college anyway, and boys who would never go, are not moved by the instrument. IV is about the others, the compliers. Imbens and Angrist (1994) called it the local average treatment effect (LATE). If those who are held back by cost gain more from school than the average, the IV estimate is higher, and it is right, for them.

Where on the ladder did the instrument push? Schooling is the sum of steps, \(s = \sum_k I(s \ge k)\), so the first stage can be split into steps:

Code 
steps <- data.frame(k = 8:18); steps$effect <- steps$se <- NA
for (i in seq_along(steps$k)) {
  co <- coef(summary(lm(
    fml(paste0("I(educ >= ", steps$k[i], ")"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)),
    card
  )))["nearc4", ]
  steps$effect[i] <- co[1]
  steps$se[i] <- co[2]
}
ggplot(steps, aes(k, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = effect - 1.96 * se, ymax = effect + 1.96 * se), colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 2.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 8:18) +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of a college nearby on reaching at least k years",
    x = "years of schooling, k",
    y = "change in the share of men"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
all_steps <- sum(sapply((min(card$educ) + 1):max(card$educ), function(k) {
  coef(lm(fml(paste0("I(educ >= ", k, ")"), paste("nearc4 +", controls)), card))[["nearc4"]]
}))
c(sum_over_all_steps = all_steps, first_stage = coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]])
sum_over_all_steps        first_stage 
         0.3198989          0.3198989
Code 
top <- steps[which.max(steps$effect), ]

The sum of the steps is the first stage, 0.32 years. The largest step is at 13 years (6.4 percentage points more men reach it). So the estimate is about boys who were near the decision for or against some college, and not about the value of the tenth year of school.

Other explanations are less flattering: measurement error in schooling pulls least squares down, the instrument may be invalid, and studies with a “significant” IV result are more easily published.

7. Can we believe the conditions?

Does the instrument predict what it should not?

Independence cannot be tested, since \(u\) is not observed. But we can check some things that the instrument should not be related to, after the controls (with age instead of experience, because experience contains schooling):

Code 
controls_age <- sub("exper + expersq", "age + I(age^2)", controls, fixed = TRUE)
check_vars <- c(
  fatheduc = "father's schooling",
  motheduc = "mother's schooling",
  momdad14 = "lived with both parents at 14",
  libcrd14 = "library card at home at 14",
  IQ = "IQ (from school records)",
  KWW = "knowledge of the world of work"
)
balance <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(check_vars), function(v) {
    m <- lm(fml(v, paste("nearc4 +", controls_age)), card)
    co <- coef(summary(m))["nearc4", ]
    data.frame(
      variable = check_vars[[v]],
      raw_difference = mean(card[[v]][card$nearc4 == 1], na.rm = TRUE) -
        mean(card[[v]][card$nearc4 == 0], na.rm = TRUE),
      with_controls = co[1],
      SE = co[2],
      p = co[4],
      n = nobs(m)
    )
  })
)
print(data.frame(balance[1], round(balance[2:5], 3), n = balance$n), row.names = FALSE)
                       variable raw_difference with_controls    SE     p    n
             father's schooling          1.135         0.280 0.177 0.113 2320
             mother's schooling          0.594        -0.016 0.144 0.913 2657
  lived with both parents at 14          0.001        -0.022 0.018 0.210 3010
     library card at home at 14          0.183         0.044 0.019 0.022 2997
       IQ (from school records)          2.596         0.904 0.752 0.229 2061
 knowledge of the world of work          2.974         0.756 0.315 0.016 2963

The controls remove most of the raw differences. What is left is small, but not nothing: 2 of the 6 have p < .05 (library card at home at 14 and knowledge of the world of work). (The last one was measured in 1966, when the men were 14 to 24 years old and a part of them had already left school, so it may partly be an effect of schooling.) Boys near a college seem to come from homes with a few more books.

Card’s own test

Card argued like this. A college nearby should matter most to boys from poor families, for whom the cost decides. So the product of “college nearby” and “parents without high school” can be the instrument, and then “college nearby” itself may go into the wage equation. If it has a direct effect on wages, it will show there. In his Table 5 the IV estimate is 0.093 (0.065) and the direct effect 0.015 (0.029). His classes of parental education are not in our file, but we can build something like them. As he did in this table, we treat experience as endogenous, with age as its instrument (the last part of this section says why):

Code 
card$fa <- ifelse(is.na(card$fatheduc), mean(card$fatheduc, na.rm = TRUE), card$fatheduc)
card$mo <- ifelse(is.na(card$motheduc), mean(card$motheduc, na.rm = TRUE), card$motheduc)
card$fa_missing <- as.numeric(is.na(card$fatheduc))
card$mo_missing <- as.numeric(is.na(card$motheduc))
family <- "fa * mo + fa_missing + mo_missing + momdad14 + sinmom14 + step14"
low_defs <- list(
  `no parent known to have 12 years` = with(
    card,
    (is.na(fatheduc) | fatheduc < 12) & (is.na(motheduc) | motheduc < 12)
  ),
  `both known, both below 12 years` = with(
    card,
    !is.na(fatheduc) & !is.na(motheduc) & fatheduc < 12 & motheduc < 12
  )
)
card_test <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(low_defs), function(k) {
    card$low <- as.numeric(low_defs[[k]])
    rest <- sub("exper + expersq", "low", controls, fixed = TRUE)
    first <- lm(fml("educ", paste("nearc4 * low + age + I(age^2) +", rest, "+", family)), card)
    m <- ivreg(
      fml(
        "lwage",
        paste(
          "educ + nearc4 + exper + expersq +",
          rest,
          "+",
          family,
          "| nearc4:low + nearc4 + age + I(age^2) +",
          rest,
          "+",
          family
        )
      ),
      data = card
    )
    data.frame(
      parents = k,
      n_low = sum(card$low),
      college_effect_others = coef(first)[["nearc4"]],
      extra_for_low = coef(first)[["nearc4:low"]],
      SE_extra = coef(summary(first))["nearc4:low", 2],
      IV = coef(m)[["educ"]],
      SE_IV = coef(summary(m))["educ", 2],
      direct_effect = coef(m)[["nearc4"]],
      SE_direct = coef(summary(m))["nearc4", 2]
    )
  })
)
tab <- t(round(card_test[-(1:2)], 3))
colnames(tab) <- card_test$parents
tab
                      no parent known to have 12 years both known, both below 12 years
college_effect_others                            0.187                           0.385
extra_for_low                                    0.339                          -0.107
SE_extra                                         0.180                           0.199
IV                                               0.133                           0.119
SE_IV                                            0.093                           0.391
direct_effect                                   -0.001                           0.004
SE_direct                                        0.038                           0.140

With the first definition (1,431 men with less educated parents) the picture is the one of Card: the college matters more for the sons of less educated parents (0.19 years for the others, 0.34 more for them), the IV estimate is 0.133 (SE 0.093), and the direct effect is -0.001 (SE 0.038). With the second definition (815 men) the extra effect has the wrong sign, and nothing can be estimated (SE of the IV estimate 0.39). The test says what Card wrote himself: “although imprecise”, there is no evidence against the instrument. That is not the same as evidence for it.

How large a violation would change the answer?

Suppose that growing up near a college raises wages directly by \(\gamma\) (better labour market, better schools). Then the right estimate would be

\[\hat\beta(\gamma) = \frac{\text{reduced form} - \gamma}{\text{first stage}}\]

(Conley et al., 2012, develop this idea.)

Code 
rf <- coef(reduced_form)[["nearc4"]]; fs <- coef(first_stage)[["nearc4"]]
gamma <- seq(0, 0.06, length.out = 100)
g_ols <- rf - coef(ols)[["educ"]] * fs
ggplot(data.frame(gamma, b = (rf - gamma) / fs), aes(gamma, b)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = coef(ols)[["educ"]], colour = "#eb6834") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.058,
    y = coef(ols)[["educ"]] + 0.008,
    label = "least squares",
    hjust = 1,
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "IV estimate, if the instrument also had a direct effect on wages",
    x = "direct effect of a college nearby on the log wage",
    y = "effect of a year of schooling"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
cbind(
  value = c(
    reduced_form = rf,
    first_stage = fs,
    gamma_for_the_OLS_result = g_ols,
    gamma_for_zero = rf
  )
)
                              value
reduced_form             0.04206794
first_stage              0.31989894
gamma_for_the_OLS_result 0.01817364
gamma_for_zero           0.04206794

A direct effect of only 1.8% on wages would bring the estimate down to the one of least squares, and one of 4.2% to zero. Because IV divides by a small first stage, small violations become large errors. And nobody can rule out a direct effect of 2%.

A control that is not innocent

exper is age − schooling − 6. It contains schooling, the very variable that we consider endogenous. Two remedies: use age instead of experience, or treat experience as endogenous too and use age as its instrument. Card did the second in his panel B of Table 3 and found 0.122 (0.046):

Code 
iv_age <- ivreg(
  fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls_age, "| nearc4 +", controls_age)),
  data = card
)
iv_exper <- ivreg(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls, "| nearc4 +", controls_age)), data = card)
ols_age  <- lm(fml("lwage", paste("educ +", controls_age)), card)
alt <- rbind(
  `OLS, experience` = coef(summary(ols))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, experience as in Card` = coef(summary(iv))["educ", 1:2],
  `OLS, age` = coef(summary(ols_age))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, age` = coef(summary(iv_age))["educ", 1:2],
  `IV, experience instrumented by age` = coef(summary(iv_exper))["educ", 1:2]
)
F_age <- summary(iv_age)$diagnostics["Weak instruments", "statistic"]
round(alt, 3); c(first_stage_F_with_age = F_age)
                                   Estimate Std. Error
OLS, experience                       0.075      0.003
IV, experience as in Card             0.132      0.055
OLS, age                              0.034      0.003
IV, age                               0.083      0.046
IV, experience instrumented by age    0.122      0.046
first_stage_F_with_age 
              11.89729

The last row gives his number. With age, the first stage is weaker (F = 11.9), and the IV estimate is 0.083 (SE = 0.046). At a given age, a man with one more year of school has one year less experience, so the two versions do not measure the same thing: with experience held constant the coefficient is larger by the value of that year of work. The choice must be made by the question, and reported.

8. Things to keep in mind

  • The instrument is an argument, not a statistic. Write down why it should be independent, and why there is no other way to the outcome.
  • Always show the first stage, the reduced form and the OLS result next to the IV result. The reduced form is an ordinary regression: if you cannot see the effect there, it is probably not there (Angrist & Krueger, 2001).
  • Weak instruments: report the (robust) first-stage F and an Anderson–Rubin interval. Many weak instruments are worse than one good one: 2SLS then moves towards OLS. (LIML is better.)
  • Do not put fitted values from a logistic first stage into a second regression. 2SLS wants linear first stages, also for a 0/1 treatment.
  • All controls belong in both stages.
  • Standard errors: use ivreg(), not the second lm(); robust or clustered by the unit to which the instrument belongs (here the county, which is not in the file).
  • LATE: the estimate is for those whom the instrument moved.
  • Measurement error in the predictor is another reason to use IV: a second, independent measurement is an instrument for the first. (With known error variances, see Deming regression.)
  • Relatives: regression with selection uses the same kind of exclusion; panel data removes what is constant over time without any instrument.

9. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the instrument and the argument for it, the controls, the first stage with its F, the reduced form, OLS and IV with standard errors, a weak-instrument-robust interval, and the group to which the estimate refers. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
row <- function(m, term) { co <- coef(summary(m))[term, ]; c(f3(co[1]), f3(co[2])) }
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Regression = c(
    "First stage (years of schooling on college nearby)",
    "Reduced form (log wage on college nearby)", "Log wage on schooling, OLS",
    "Log wage on schooling, 2SLS", "Log wage on schooling, 2SLS, two instruments"
  ),
  rbind(
    row(first_stage, "nearc4"),
    row(reduced_form, "nearc4"),
    row(ols, "educ"),
    row(iv, "educ"),
    row(iv2, "educ")
  )
)
names(apa_table) <- c("Regression", "b", "SE")
apa_table$CI <- c(apply(
  rbind(
    confint(first_stage)["nearc4", ],
    confint(reduced_form)["nearc4", ],
    confint(ols)["educ", ],
    ci_iv,
    confint(iv2)["educ", ]
  ),
  1,
  function(v) paste0("[", f3(v[1]), ", ", f3(v[2]), "]")
))

Method (data analysis):

The return to schooling was estimated for 3,010 men of the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men (log hourly wage in 1976; Card, 1993). Because unobserved ability and family background may influence both schooling and wages, schooling was instrumented with the presence of a four-year college in the local labour market of residence in 1966, which lowered the cost of college for boys who could live at home. All models contained experience, experience squared, and indicators for black, residence in the south, metropolitan residence in 1966 and 1976, and region in 1966. Two-stage least squares was used (R package ivreg); the strength of the instrument was judged with the first-stage F, and a 95% Anderson–Rubin interval (Anderson & Rubin, 1949) was computed because it is valid with weak instruments. Endogeneity was tested with the Wu–Hausman test, and the robustness of the result to a direct effect of the instrument was examined (Conley et al., 2012). Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026).

Results:

After adjustment for the controls, men who grew up near a college had 0.32 more years of schooling (SE = 0.09, F(1, 2,994) = 13.3, p < .001) and 4.3% higher wages (log wage: b = 0.042, SE = 0.018, p = .020; Table 1). The two-stage least squares estimate of the effect of one year of schooling on the log wage was b = 0.132 (SE = 0.055, p = .017), 95% Anderson–Rubin CI [0.025, 0.285], compared with 0.075 (SE = 0.003) with ordinary least squares. The Wu–Hausman test did not distinguish the two, F(1, 2,993) = 1.17, p = .280. A direct effect of the instrument of 1.8% on wages would suffice to reduce the estimate to that of least squares.

Table 1

Schooling and Log Wages of 3,010 Young Men, With a College Nearby as Instrument

Regression b SE 95% CI
First stage (years of schooling on college nearby) 0.320 0.088 [0.148, 0.492]
Reduced form (log wage on college nearby) 0.042 0.018 [0.007, 0.078]
Log wage on schooling, OLS 0.075 0.003 [0.068, 0.082]
Log wage on schooling, 2SLS 0.132 0.055 [0.024, 0.239]
Log wage on schooling, 2SLS, two instruments 0.157 0.053 [0.054, 0.260]

Note. All models contain the controls named in the text. The confidence intervals are the usual ones; the Anderson–Rubin interval for the fourth row is [0.025, 0.285]. Two instruments: four-year and two-year college nearby (Sargan test p = .264).

Points to remember:

  • Argue for the instrument before showing numbers.
  • Report the first stage, the reduced form, OLS and IV together.
  • Give the first-stage F and an interval that is valid for weak instruments.
  • Say for whom the estimate holds, and how large a violation would change it.

10. Summary

When A predictor is related to something unseen that also affects the outcome, and there is a source of variation that is not
Conditions Relevance (testable), independence, exclusion (not testable), monotonicity
One 0/1 instrument Difference in the outcome, divided by the difference in the predictor
In general Two-stage least squares, \(\hat\beta = (W^\top P_Z W)^{-1}W^\top P_Z y\)
How (R) ivreg(y ~ x + controls | z + controls); also fixest::feols()
Check First-stage F, Wu–Hausman, Sargan (with extra instruments), balance, sensitivity
Interval Anderson–Rubin when the instrument is not very strong
Meaning The effect for those whom the instrument moved (LATE)
Related pages Simple regression, selection models, panel data

References

Anderson, T. W., & Rubin, H. (1949). Estimation of the parameters of a single equation in a complete system of stochastic equations. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 20(1), 46–63. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177730090

Angrist, J., & Kolesár, M. (2024). One instrument to rule them all: The bias and coverage of just-ID IV. Journal of Econometrics, 240(2), Article 105398. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2022.12.012

Angrist, J. D., & Krueger, A. B. (2001). Instrumental variables and the search for identification: From supply and demand to natural experiments. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 15(4), 69–85. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.15.4.69

Card, D. (1993). Using geographic variation in college proximity to estimate the return to schooling (NBER Working Paper No. 4483). National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w4483

Conley, T. G., Hansen, C. B., & Rossi, P. E. (2012). Plausibly exogenous. Review of Economics and Statistics, 94(1), 260–272. https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00139

Imbens, G. W., & Angrist, J. D. (1994). Identification and estimation of local average treatment effects. Econometrica, 62(2), 467–475. https://doi.org/10.2307/2951620

Lee, D. S., McCrary, J., Moreira, M. J., & Porter, J. (2022). Valid t-ratio inference for IV. American Economic Review, 112(10), 3260–3290. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20211063

Staiger, D., & Stock, J. H. (1997). Instrumental variables regression with weak instruments. Econometrica, 65(3), 557–586. https://doi.org/10.2307/2171753

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Neural Network Regression: How Much Power Will the Plant Deliver?
item.description: Neural network regression in R with nnet, on 9,568 hours of a power plant (UCI): what a neuron is, how bent lines add up to any curve, the loss with weight decay, backpropagation written by hand and checked against numerical derivatives, the same minimum as nnet, two classic mistakes, many starts and many different answers, overfitting on forty rows, choosing the size with cross-validation, why random folds flatter methods that remember, a comparison with a straight line, a GAM, nearest neighbours and a random forest on conditions that were left out, what the network has learned, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Neural network regression in R with nnet, on 9,568 hours of a power plant (UCI): what a neuron is, how bent lines add up to any curve, the loss with weight decay, backpropagation written by hand and checked against numerical derivatives, the same minimum as nnet, two classic mistakes, many starts and many different answers, overfitting on forty rows, choosing the size with cross-validation, why random folds flatter methods that remember, a comparison with a straight line, a GAM, nearest neighbours and a random forest on conditions that were left out, what the network has learned, and APA reporting.

The question: many bent lines

A straight line is the wrong shape for most things. Splines bend it, one predictor at a time. A neural network goes further: it adds up many little bent lines, each of which looks at all predictors at once, and it finds out by itself where to bend and which predictors to combine.

That sounds like magic and is ordinary regression: there are parameters (called weights), there is a sum of squared errors, and a computer makes the sum small. The site’s page about handwritten digits uses networks to sort things into classes. Here the network predicts a number: the electrical power of a plant from the weather.

This page writes a network by hand, derivatives included, and finds the same solution as the package. Then it asks the question that matters more than the method: what is a fair test? The answer changes the ranking of the methods.

Code 
library(ggplot2)
library(nnet)        # nnet(): networks with one hidden layer (comes with R)
library(mgcv)        # bam(): a GAM, to compare with
# also used, with package::function: readxl (read_excel), ranger (ranger), FNN (knn.reg)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
num  <- function(x) trimws(format(x, big.mark = ","))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))

1. The data

Code 
zip_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file(
  "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/294/combined+cycle+power+plant.zip",
  zip_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE
)
files <- unzip(zip_file, exdir = tempfile("ccpp"))
raw   <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(grep("xlsx$", files, value = TRUE), sheet = 1))
names(raw) <- c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity", "power")
c(rows = nrow(raw), exact_copies = sum(duplicated(raw)))
        rows exact_copies 
        9568           41
Code 
plant <- unique(raw)
summary(plant)
  temperature        vacuum         pressure         humidity          power      
 Min.   : 1.81   Min.   :25.36   Min.   : 992.9   Min.   : 25.56   Min.   :420.3  
 1st Qu.:13.53   1st Qu.:41.74   1st Qu.:1009.1   1st Qu.: 63.38   1st Qu.:439.8  
 Median :20.35   Median :52.08   Median :1012.9   Median : 75.00   Median :451.5  
 Mean   :19.66   Mean   :54.29   Mean   :1013.2   Mean   : 73.33   Mean   :454.3  
 3rd Qu.:25.71   3rd Qu.:66.51   3rd Qu.:1017.2   3rd Qu.: 84.85   3rd Qu.:468.4  
 Max.   :37.11   Max.   :81.56   Max.   :1033.3   Max.   :100.16   Max.   :495.8

The data come from a combined cycle power plant (Tüfekci, 2014; Tüfekci & Kaya, 2014), in which gas turbines and a steam turbine work together. Each row is the average of one hour at full load, between 2006 and 2011. The outcome is the net electrical power (MW). The predictors are the temperature of the air (°C), the pressure of the air (mbar), the relative humidity (%), and the exhaust vacuum of the steam turbine (cm Hg). 41 rows are exact copies of others; we drop them, so that no row can be in the training data and in the test at once. 9,527 are left.

Two details of this file will matter later. The file has been shuffled, and there is no date. And the vacuum takes only 634 different values, although it is given with two decimals.

2. Look at the data

Code 
set.seed(201); some <- plant[sample(nrow(plant), 2000), ]
long <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity"), function(v) {
    data.frame(predictor = v, x = some[[v]], power = some$power)
  })
)
ggplot(long, aes(x, power)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Power against each predictor",
    subtitle = "2,000 of the hours",
    x = NULL,
    y = "power (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
round(cor(plant), 2)
            temperature vacuum pressure humidity power
temperature        1.00   0.84    -0.51    -0.54 -0.95
vacuum             0.84   1.00    -0.42    -0.31 -0.87
pressure          -0.51  -0.42     1.00     0.10  0.52
humidity          -0.54  -0.31     0.10     1.00  0.39
power             -0.95  -0.87     0.52     0.39  1.00

Warm air is thin, and a gas turbine gets less of it: temperature alone has a correlation of -0.95 with power. The relationship is nearly straight, with a bend. So a straight line will already do well, and a network can only win by details.

3. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: standardise

Every variable gets mean 0 and SD 1 (with the mean and SD of the training data). Weights of different predictors then have comparable sizes, and the search starts in a sensible region.

Code 
standardise <- function(train, d) as.data.frame(scale(d, colMeans(train), apply(train, 2, sd)))
z <- standardise(plant, plant)
X <- as.matrix(z[, c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity")]); y <- z$power

Step 2: one neuron

A neuron takes a weighted sum of the predictors and sends it through an S-shaped function, the logistic function \(\sigma(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})\), the one from logistic regression:

\[h = \sigma(a_0 + a_1 x_1 + \dots + a_K x_K)\]

It is flat on the left, flat on the right and rises in between. The weights decide where the rise is, how steep, and in which direction.

Step 3: the network

The hidden layer has \(J\) neurons. The output is a linear regression on them:

\[\hat y = b_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{J} b_j\, \sigma\!\Big(a_{0j} + \sum_{k=1}^K a_{kj} x_k\Big)\]

That makes \(J(K + 1) + J + 1\) weights: with 4 predictors and 10 neurons, 61. Already a few S-curves add up to all kinds of shapes:

Code 
x1 <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)
parts <- data.frame(
  x = rep(x1, 3),
  h = c(1.6 * plogis(-4 + 6 * x1), -2.2 * plogis(1 + 3 * x1), 1.5 * plogis(5 + 4 * x1)),
  neuron = rep(paste("neuron", 1:3), each = 200)
)
ggplot(parts, aes(x, h)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = neuron), linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(x = x1, h = tapply(parts$h, rep(1:200, 3), sum)), linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Three neurons (dashed) and their sum (black)", x = "x", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()

With enough neurons such a sum can come as close as you like to any continuous function (Hornik et al., 1989). That is a statement about what is possible. It does not say how many neurons or how much data you need, nor that the search will find it.

Step 4: the loss

As in least squares, with a penalty for large weights, called weight decay (\(\lambda\)). It is the penalty of ridge regression:

\[E(w) = \sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 + \lambda \sum w^2\]

Step 5: the derivatives (backpropagation)

To go downhill one needs the slope of \(E\) in the direction of every weight. The chain rule gives it, from the output backwards (Rumelhart et al., 1986). With \(r_i = -2(y_i - \hat y_i)\) and the output of neuron \(j\) for row \(i\), \(h_{ij}\):

\[\frac{\partial E}{\partial b_j} = \sum_i r_i\, h_{ij} + 2\lambda b_j, \qquad \frac{\partial E}{\partial a_{kj}} = \sum_i \underbrace{r_i\, b_j\, h_{ij}(1 - h_{ij})}_{\text{the error of neuron } j}\, x_{ik} + 2\lambda a_{kj}\]

Code 
forward <- function(w, X, J) {
  # weights in the order that nnet uses
  K <- ncol(X)
  A <- matrix(w[1:(J * (K + 1))], K + 1)
  b <- w[-(1:(J * (K + 1)))]
  h <- plogis(cbind(1, X) %*% A)
  list(h = h, b = b, yhat = drop(cbind(1, h) %*% b))
}
loss <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) sum((y - forward(w, X, J)$yhat)^2) + decay * sum(w^2)
gradient <- function(w, X, y, J, decay) {
  f <- forward(w, X, J); r <- -2 * (y - f$yhat)
  neuron_error <- (r %o% f$b[-1]) * f$h * (1 - f$h)
  c(crossprod(cbind(1, X), neuron_error), crossprod(cbind(1, f$h), r)) + 2 * decay * w
}
set.seed(202)
w0 <- runif(2 * 5 + 3, -0.7, 0.7) # 2 neurons, 13 weights, a random start
numeric_slope <- sapply(seq_along(w0), function(i) {
  d <- replace(numeric(13), i, 1e-5)
  (loss(w0 + d, X, y, 2, 0.1) - loss(w0 - d, X, y, 2, 0.1)) / 2e-5
})
max(abs(numeric_slope / gradient(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1) - 1))                    # relative difference
[1] 3.351439e-10

The formula and the numerical slopes agree. (Always do this check when you write derivatives yourself.)

Step 6: go downhill

R’s optimiser optim() does the walking. nnet() gets the same start, so that we can compare:

Code 
by_hand <- optim(
  w0,
  loss,
  gradient,
  X = X,
  y = y,
  J = 2,
  decay = 0.1,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 1000, abstol = 1e-4, reltol = 1e-8)
)
package <- nnet(X, y, size = 2, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, Wts = w0, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
cbind(
  value = c(
    loss_at_the_start = loss(w0, X, y, 2, 0.1),
    loss_by_hand = by_hand$value,
    loss_nnet = package$value,
    largest_difference_in_the_weights = max(abs(by_hand$par - package$wts))
  )
)
                                         value
loss_at_the_start                 1.928871e+04
loss_by_hand                      5.797301e+02
loss_nnet                         5.797300e+02
largest_difference_in_the_weights 1.312188e-04

The two arrive at the same place.

Two classic mistakes

Code 
set.seed(203)
forgot_scaling <- nnet(power ~ ., plant, size = 10, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
forgot_linout  <- nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
c(
  SD_of_power = sd(plant$power),
  RMSE_without_scaling = rmse(predict(forgot_scaling, plant), plant$power),
  RMSE_without_linout = sd(plant$power) * rmse(predict(forgot_linout, z), z$power)
)
         SD_of_power RMSE_without_scaling  RMSE_without_linout 
            17.03908             17.03819             17.03819
Code 
rbind(
  predictions_without_linout = range(predict(forgot_linout, z)),
  outcome_standardised = range(z$power)
)
                                [,1]     [,2]
predictions_without_linout  0.000000 0.000000
outcome_standardised       -1.999868 2.431122

Without standardising, the weighted sums are in the thousands, every neuron is stuck on its flat part, and the network predicts the mean (RMSE 17.0 MW, the SD of power). Without linout = TRUE the output itself goes through the S-function and cannot leave the interval from 0 to 1; here every prediction is 0. No error message in either case.

4. Different starts, different answers

A network has many minima. First on forty rows, with temperature as the only predictor, so that we can see the curves:

Code 
set.seed(204)
forty <- z[sample(nrow(z), 40), ]
grid <- data.frame(temperature = seq(-2.6, 2.9, length.out = 300))
curves <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c(0, 0.1), function(dc) {
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:4, function(s) {
        set.seed(s)
        m <- nnet(
          power ~ temperature,
          forty,
          size = 15,
          decay = dc,
          linout = TRUE,
          trace = FALSE,
          maxit = 2000
        )
        data.frame(
          temperature = grid$temperature,
          power = drop(predict(m, grid)),
          start = s,
          train_rmse = rmse(predict(m, forty), forty$power),
          setting = ifelse(dc == 0, "no decay", "decay 0.1")
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
back <- function(v, name) v * sd(plant[[name]]) + mean(plant[[name]])
ggplot(
  curves,
  aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power"), group = start, colour = factor(start))
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    data = forty,
    aes(back(temperature, "temperature"), back(power, "power")),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~setting) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(415, 505)) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "15 neurons on 40 hours, four random starts each",
    x = "temperature (°C)",
    y = "power (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
aggregate(train_rmse ~ setting, curves, function(v) round(range(v) * sd(plant$power), 2))
    setting train_rmse.1 train_rmse.2
1 decay 0.1         3.95         3.95
2  no decay         1.58         2.46

With 46 weights and 40 points the network without decay runs through the gaps as it likes: four starts, four curves, and the differences are largest where there are few data. A little decay makes the four curves the same. Now with all rows and all predictors:

Code 
fits <- lapply(1:6, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = 10, decay = 0.1, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 600)
})
loss_values <- sapply(fits, function(m) m$value)
preds <- sapply(fits, function(m) back(drop(predict(m, z)), "power"))
round(loss_values, 1)
[1] 542.3 544.7 545.7 544.7 542.4 545.8
Code 
cbind(
  value = c(
    largest_difference_in_a_weight = max(apply(sapply(fits, function(m) m$wts), 1, function(v) {
      diff(range(v))
    })),
    typical_SD_between_the_predictions = mean(apply(preds, 1, sd)),
    RMSE_of_the_first = rmse(preds[, 1], plant$power)
  )
)
                                       value
largest_difference_in_a_weight     5.9772949
typical_SD_between_the_predictions 0.4560367
RMSE_of_the_first                  4.0272418

Six starts end at different places (loss between 542.3 and 545.8), with quite different weights. But the predictions differ by only 0.46 MW on average. So single weights mean nothing, and nobody should interpret them. The predictions are what one can use. Averaging the predictions of several networks (an ensemble) makes them more stable; section 6 shows by how much.

5. What is a fair test?

How many neurons? The usual recipe is cross-validation with random folds. But look at the data again. 99.5% of the rows share their value of the vacuum, to two decimals, with other rows: 634 values in 9,527 hours. The most likely explanation is that the vacuum was recorded less often than the rest, and that rows with the same value come from the same period. The file does not say, and its order is destroyed. But if so, then random folds put hours of the same period in the training data and in the test. A method that remembers its neighbours would be rewarded for remembering.

So we use two kinds of folds: random rows, and whole groups of rows with the same vacuum, so that the test has conditions that the model has never seen.

Code 
set.seed(205)
group   <- as.integer(factor(plant$vacuum)); n_group <- max(group)
folds3 <- list(
  random = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:3, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
net_predict <- function(train, test, size, decay, starts = 1, maxit = 400) {
  a <- standardise(train, train)
  b <- standardise(train, test)
  p <- sapply(starts, function(s) {
    set.seed(s)
    drop(predict(
      nnet(
        power ~ .,
        a,
        size = size,
        decay = decay,
        linout = TRUE,
        trace = FALSE,
        maxit = maxit,
        MaxNWts = 5000
      ),
      b
    ))
  })
  mean(train$power) + sd(train$power) * p
}
grid <- expand.grid(size = c(2, 5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.01, 0.1, 1))
cv <- do.call(
  cbind,
  lapply(folds3, function(f) {
    sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
      e <- numeric(nrow(plant))
      for (k in 1:3) {
        e[f == k] <- net_predict(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ], grid$size[i], grid$decay[i])[,
          1
        ] -
          plant$power[f == k]
      }
      sqrt(mean(e^2))
    })
  })
)
print(round(cbind(grid, cv), 3), row.names = FALSE)
 size decay random new conditions
    2  0.01  4.203          4.251
    5  0.01  4.167          4.277
   10  0.01  4.048          4.306
   20  0.01  3.970          4.368
    2  0.10  4.202          4.251
    5  0.10  4.169          4.272
   10  0.10  4.066          4.300
   20  0.10  4.015          4.322
    2  1.00  4.213          4.271
    5  1.00  4.202          4.286
   10  1.00  4.198          4.280
   20  1.00  4.184          4.276
Code 
cv_long <- data.frame(
  size = rep(grid$size, 2),
  decay = factor(rep(grid$decay, 2)),
  rmse = as.vector(cv),
  folds = rep(colnames(cv), each = nrow(grid))
)
ggplot(cv_long, aes(size, rmse, colour = decay)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(2, 5, 10, 20)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of the network against its size, for two kinds of folds",
    x = "neurons",
    y = "RMSE (MW)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
best_r <- grid[which.min(cv[, "random"]), ]; best_g <- grid[which.min(cv[, "new conditions"]), ]
rbind(
  random = cbind(best_r, rmse = min(cv[, "random"])),
  `new conditions` = cbind(best_g, rmse = min(cv[, "new conditions"]))
)
               size decay     rmse
random           20  0.01 3.969926
new conditions    2  0.10 4.250756

With random folds the larger networks keep getting better, and the best has 20 neurons and a decay of 0.01. With new conditions they get worse, unless a strong decay holds them back, and the best has 2 neurons. All settings lie between 4.25 and 4.37 MW. What the larger networks gained with random folds was mostly memory of the vacuum values in the data.

6. The network against others

Both kinds of folds again, with new folds, for seven methods: a straight line, a GAM, the 5 nearest neighbours, a random forest, the small network that the second kind of folds chose (2 neurons, decay 0.1), the large one that random folds chose (20 neurons, decay 0.01), and the average of three such large networks.

Code 
set.seed(206)
folds5 <- list(
  `random folds` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(plant))),
  `new conditions` = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_group))[group]
)
methods <- function(train, test) {
  zt <- standardise(train, train)
  zn <- standardise(train, test)
  large <- net_predict(train, test, best_r$size, best_r$decay, starts = 1:3)
  cbind(
    `straight line` = predict(lm(power ~ ., train), test),
    GAM = as.numeric(predict(
      bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = train),
      test
    )),
    `nearest neighbours` = FNN::knn.reg(zt[, 1:4], zn[, 1:4], train$power, k = 5)$pred,
    `random forest` = predict(
      ranger::ranger(power ~ ., train, num.trees = 300, seed = 1),
      test
    )$predictions,
    `small network` = net_predict(train, test, best_g$size, best_g$decay)[, 1],
    `large network` = large[, 1],
    `3 large networks, averaged` = rowMeans(large)
  )
}
results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(names(folds5), function(kind) {
    f <- folds5[[kind]]
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(1:5, function(k) {
        p <- methods(plant[f != k, ], plant[f == k, ])
        data.frame(
          folds = kind,
          fold = k,
          method = colnames(p),
          rmse = apply(p, 2, rmse, plant$power[f == k]),
          mse = apply(p, 2, function(v) sum((v - plant$power[f == k])^2))
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
total <- aggregate(mse ~ method + folds, results, sum); total$rmse <- sqrt(total$mse / nrow(plant))
wide <- reshape(
  total[, c("method", "folds", "rmse")],
  idvar = "method",
  timevar = "folds",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(wide) <- c("method", "new", "random")
wide <- wide[order(wide$new), ]
print(
  data.frame(
    method = wide$method,
    random_folds = round(wide$random, 2),
    new_conditions = round(wide$new, 2)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
)
                     method random_folds new_conditions
 3 large networks, averaged         3.90           4.21
              small network         4.20           4.23
                        GAM         4.17           4.24
              large network         3.96           4.33
              random forest         3.22           4.43
              straight line         4.56           4.58
         nearest neighbours         3.79           4.80
Code 
results$method <- factor(results$method, levels = rev(wide$method[order(wide$random)]))
ggplot(results, aes(rmse, method)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = transform(total, method = factor(method, levels = levels(results$method))),
    colour = "#eb6834",
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~folds) +
  labs(
    title = "Error of seven methods, two kinds of folds",
    subtitle = "Orange: all rows. Blue: single folds",
    x = "RMSE (MW)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
Code 
w  <- function(m, v) wide[[v]][wide$method == m]
by_fold <- function(m) subset(results, folds == "new conditions" & method == m)$rmse
cbind(
  value = c(
    folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest = sum(
      by_fold("small network") < by_fold("random forest")
    ),
    folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network = sum(
      by_fold("3 large networks, averaged") < by_fold("large network")
    )
  )
)
                                                   value
folds_in_which_the_small_network_beats_the_forest      4
folds_in_which_the_average_beats_one_large_network     4
  • With random folds the random forest wins by far: 3.22 MW, against 3.90 for the averaged large networks, 4.17 for the GAM and 4.56 for the straight line. (In the paper that introduced the data, bagged trees came first among many methods, with an RMSE of 3.79 MW and folds of shuffled rows; Tüfekci, 2014.)
  • With new conditions the order is another one. The averaged large networks (4.21), the small network (4.23) and the GAM (4.24) are practically tied; the forest has 4.43, the straight line 4.58. The small network beats the forest in 4 of the 5 folds. The nearest neighbours, which were well ahead of the straight line before, are the last with 4.80.
  • The stiff methods (straight line, GAM, small network) have nearly the same error in both tests, for example 4.17 and 4.24 for the GAM. They cannot remember single periods. The flexible ones lose a lot: the forest goes from 3.22 to 4.43, the large network from 3.96 to 4.33.
  • Averaging three large networks changed the error from 4.33 to 4.21 (new conditions) and from 3.96 to 3.90 (random folds): it helped, at three times the cost.

Which of the two tests is right? It depends on the use. To fill a missing hour in the past, random folds. To forecast the power of next week, the second, and even that may be too kind, since vacuum values close to the left-out ones are still in the training data. Choose the folds so that the test is like the use.

The gain from all that flexibility is modest here. From the straight line to the best method with new conditions, the RMSE falls from 4.58 to 4.21 MW.

7. What has the network learned?

The partial dependence of a predictor: set it to a value in every row, predict, and average. For three large networks, the small one and the GAM:

Code 
set.seed(207); bg <- plant[sample(nrow(plant), 400), ]; zbg <- standardise(plant, bg)
one_net <- function(size, decay, s) {
  set.seed(s)
  nnet(power ~ ., z, size = size, decay = decay, linout = TRUE, trace = FALSE, maxit = 400)
}
nets <- c(
  lapply(1:3, function(s) one_net(best_r$size, best_r$decay, s)),
  list(one_net(best_g$size, best_g$decay, 1))
)
gam_all <- bam(power ~ s(temperature) + s(vacuum) + s(pressure) + s(humidity), data = plant)
pd <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "pressure", "humidity"), function(v) {
    q <- seq(quantile(plant[[v]], 0.01), quantile(plant[[v]], 0.99), length.out = 25)
    do.call(
      rbind,
      lapply(q, function(x0) {
        b2 <- bg
        b2[[v]] <- x0
        zb <- standardise(plant, b2)
        data.frame(
          predictor = v,
          x = x0,
          model = c(paste("large", 1:3), "small", "GAM"),
          power = c(
            sapply(nets, function(m) mean(back(drop(predict(m, zb)), "power"))),
            mean(predict(gam_all, b2))
          )
        )
      })
    )
  })
)
pd$kind <- factor(
  ifelse(
    grepl("large", pd$model),
    "three large networks",
    ifelse(pd$model == "small", "small network", "GAM")
  ),
  levels = c("three large networks", "small network", "GAM")
)
ggplot(pd, aes(x, power, group = model, colour = kind, linewidth = kind)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(0.5, 1, 1), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Partial dependence of power on each predictor", x = NULL, y = "power (MW)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
span <- function(v, m) { p <- subset(pd, predictor == v & model == m); diff(range(p$power)) }
spans <- sapply(c("temperature", "vacuum", "humidity", "pressure"), function(v) {
  sapply(c("small", "GAM", "large 1"), function(m) span(v, m))
})
round(spans, 1)
        temperature vacuum humidity pressure
small          50.9   11.3      6.3      4.4
GAM            48.3   10.3      6.7      2.9
large 1        42.5   15.0      7.2      2.5

In the small network, temperature moves the power by 50.9 MW over its range (from the 1st to the 99th percentile), the vacuum by 11.3, humidity by 6.3 and air pressure by 4.4.
