Cortes, C., & Vapnik, V. (1995). Support-vector networks. Machine Learning, 20(3), 273–297. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00994018

Smola, A. J., & Schölkopf, B. (2004). A tutorial on support vector regression. Statistics and Computing, 14(3), 199–222. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:STCO.0000035301.49549.88

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Spatial Regression: Do Regions Catch Unemployment From Their Neighbours?
item.description: Spatial regression in R with spdep and spatialreg, on unemployment, education and income in about 230 European regions (Eurostat, 2019): neighbours and weights, Moran’s I, what spatial correlation does to least squares, the spatial lag and the spatial error model by hand, Lagrange multiplier tests, direct and indirect impacts, the spatial Durbin model, what remains once countries are in the model, sensitivity to the weights, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Spatial regression in R with spdep and spatialreg, on unemployment, education and income in about 230 European regions (Eurostat, 2019): neighbours and weights, Moran’s I, what spatial correlation does to least squares, the spatial lag and the spatial error model by hand, Lagrange multiplier tests, direct and indirect impacts, the spatial Durbin model, what remains once countries are in the model, sensitivity to the weights, and APA reporting.

The question: the map is not random

Look at a map of unemployment in Europe, and the colours come in patches. Regions with many unemployed lie next to each other, and so do those with few. A region of southern Spain looks like the region beside it, whatever its schools and its income.

This matters for two reasons. Statistically, regions are not independent observations: neighbours repeat each other’s information, and the standard errors of ordinary regression are too small. Substantively, the patches may be a result in themselves. Perhaps unemployment spreads: people commute across the border, firms sell to the region next door, and a closed factory hurts both sides.

Spatial regression puts the neighbours into the model. This page fits the two classic models, shows how to read them (their coefficients are not the effects), and asks at the end what the patches really are.

Code 
library(jsonlite)     # Eurostat answers in JSON
library(sf)           # maps
library(spdep)        # neighbours, Moran's I, Lagrange multiplier tests
library(spatialreg)   # spatial regression models
library(ggplot2)
# number formats for the text
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

1. The data

Eurostat publishes statistics for the NUTS-2 regions of Europe, and the maps that belong to them. Both are free and need no login. We use 2019, the last year before the pandemic.

Code 
eurostat <- function(code, query) {
  j <- fromJSON(paste0(
    "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/",
    code,
    "?format=JSON&lang=EN&geoLevel=nuts2&time=2019&",
    query
  ))
  place <- unlist(j$dimension$geo$category$index)
  value <- unlist(j$value)
  data.frame(
    NUTS_ID = names(place),
    value = unname(value[match(as.character(place), names(value))])
  )
}
unemp <- eurostat("lfst_r_lfu3rt", "sex=T&age=Y15-74") # unemployment rate (%)
# adults with tertiary education (%)
degree <- eurostat("edat_lfse_04", "sex=T&age=Y25-64&isced11=ED5-8")
# GDP per head, purchasing power standards
gdp <- eurostat("nama_10r_2gdp", "unit=PPS_EU27_2020_HAB")
map <- st_read(
  "https://gisco-services.ec.europa.eu/distribution/v2/nuts/geojson/NUTS_RG_20M_2016_4326_LEVL_2.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
)
map$unemp  <- unemp$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, unemp$NUTS_ID)]
map$degree <- degree$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, degree$NUTS_ID)]
map$gdp    <- gdp$value[match(map$NUTS_ID, gdp$NUTS_ID)]
map <- st_transform(
  subset(map, !is.na(unemp) & !is.na(degree) & !is.na(gdp) & CNTR_CODE != "TR"),
  3035
) # a projection in metres
xy  <- st_coordinates(suppressWarnings(st_centroid(map)))
# without the islands far away (Canaries, Azores, overseas)
europe <- map[xy[, 1] > 2.5e6 & xy[, 2] > 1.3e6, ]
xy  <- st_coordinates(suppressWarnings(st_centroid(europe)))
d   <- st_drop_geometry(europe)
d$log_u <- log(d$unemp); d$log_gdp <- log(d$gdp / 30000); d$deg10 <- (d$degree - 33) / 10
c(regions = nrow(d), countries = length(unique(d$CNTR_CODE)))
  regions countries 
      234        31
Code 
round(
  sapply(d[, c("unemp", "degree", "gdp")], function(v) {
    c(min = min(v), median = median(v), max = max(v))
  }),
  1
)
       unemp degree   gdp
min      1.3   11.7  8500
median   5.1   30.1 28100
max     27.0   56.1 78700

There are 234 regions of 31 countries. The unemployment rate goes from 1.3% to 27.0%. Because it is skewed, we use its logarithm. deg10 is the share of adults with a degree, in steps of 10 points from 33%, and log_gdp the log of the income per head, relative to 30,000.

2. Look at the map

Code 
ggplot(europe) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = unemp), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "B",
    direction = -1,
    trans = "log",
    breaks = c(2, 4, 8, 16),
    name = "%"
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(2.5e6, 6e6), ylim = c(1.4e6, 5.3e6)) +
  labs(title = "Unemployment in the regions of Europe, 2019") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

Who is whose neighbour?

A spatial model needs a definition of neighbours, the weights matrix \(W\). Regions that share a border is one choice, but islands have none. We take the five nearest regions (by the distance of their centres), and give each the weight 1/5. The rows of \(W\) sum to 1, so \(Wy\) is the mean of the neighbours of each region, the spatial lag of \(y\).

Code 
W <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 5)), style = "W")
d$lag_u <- lag.listw(W, d$log_u)                        # the mean of the five neighbours
moran <- moran.test(d$log_u, W)
moran$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]]
[1] 0.7208608
Code 
ggplot(d, aes(log_u, lag_u)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#eb6834") +
  labs(
    title = "Each region and the mean of its five neighbours",
    x = "log unemployment of the region",
    y = "mean of its neighbours"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Moran’s I is a correlation between a region and its neighbours: the slope of the line in this chart. It is 0.72, where 0 would be no pattern. Unemployment is strongly clustered.

3. What it does to least squares

Code 
ols <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d)
round(coef(summary(ols)), 3)
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    1.648      0.040  40.714        0
deg10          0.193      0.052   3.744        0
log_gdp       -0.920      0.125  -7.378        0
Code 
mr <- lm.morantest(ols, W)
c(Moran_I_of_the_residuals = mr$estimate[[1]], p = mr$p.value[[1]])
Moran_I_of_the_residuals                        p 
            6.727311e-01             2.783120e-72

OLS finds that richer regions have less unemployment (-0.92: 10% more income, 8.4% less unemployment) and, oddly, that regions with more graduates have more of it, once income is held constant. Both are “highly significant”. But the residuals have a Moran’s I of 0.67: the model has explained almost nothing of the map. The 234 regions are not 234 independent pieces of information, and neither result can be trusted.

4. The two classic models, with formulas

The spatial lag model (SAR)

\[y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon\]

The unemployment of the neighbours is a cause of the region’s own. It is a story of contagion, and a circle: my neighbour’s unemployment depends on mine, too. Solved for \(y\):

\[y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}(X\beta + \varepsilon)\]

A change in one region travels to its neighbours, to their neighbours, and back.

The spatial error model (SEM)

\[y = X\beta + u, \qquad u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon\]

Here the neighbours do not act on each other. They share unmeasured things, such as history, industry, and laws, which are in the error. OLS is unbiased, and only its standard errors are wrong. It is the spatial cousin of GLS with autocorrelated errors.

Why not just put \(Wy\) into lm()?

Because of the circle. \(Wy\) is correlated with the error. Maximum likelihood takes it into account with one extra term, the log of the determinant of \(I - \rho W\):

\[\log L = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \log|I - \rho W| - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert y - \rho Wy - X\beta \rVert^2\]

For a given \(\rho\), \(\beta\) is an ordinary regression of \(y - \rho Wy\) on \(X\). So we need to search over \(\rho\) only:

Code 
y <- d$log_u; X <- model.matrix(ols); n <- nrow(X)
Wm <- listw2mat(W); Wy <- drop(Wm %*% y); ev <- eigen(Wm, only.values = TRUE)$values
profile_ll <- function(rho) {
  e <- lm.fit(X, y - rho * Wy)$residuals
  -n / 2 * (log(2 * pi * mean(e^2)) + 1) + sum(Re(log(as.complex(1 - rho * ev))))
}
rho_hat <- optimize(profile_ll, c(-0.9, 0.99), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
sar <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W)
naive <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + lag_u, data = d)
rbind(
  by_hand = c(rho = rho_hat, lm.fit(X, y - rho_hat * Wy)$coefficients),
  lagsarlm = c(sar$rho, sar$coefficients),
  `wrong: lm with the lag` = coef(naive)[c(4, 1:3)]
)
                             rho (Intercept)      deg10    log_gdp
by_hand                0.7641734   0.3782375 0.05019551 -0.3730810
lagsarlm               0.7641573   0.3782643 0.05019852 -0.3730925
wrong: lm with the lag 0.8874702   0.1733785 0.02712854 -0.2847873

5. Fitting the models and reading the output

Code 
sem  <- errorsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W)
# with the neighbours' X as well
sdm <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = W, Durbin = TRUE)
tab <- rbind(
  OLS = c(coef(summary(ols))[2, 1:2], coef(summary(ols))[3, 1:2], NA, AIC(ols)),
  `spatial lag` = c(summary(sar)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sar)$Coef[3, 1:2], sar$rho, AIC(sar)),
  `spatial error` = c(summary(sem)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sem)$Coef[3, 1:2], sem$lambda, AIC(sem)),
  `spatial Durbin` = c(summary(sdm)$Coef[2, 1:2], summary(sdm)$Coef[3, 1:2], sdm$rho, AIC(sdm))
)
colnames(tab) <- c("deg10", "SE", "log_gdp", "SE", "rho or lambda", "AIC")
round(tab, 3)
               deg10    SE log_gdp    SE rho or lambda     AIC
OLS            0.193 0.052  -0.920 0.125            NA 431.684
spatial lag    0.050 0.033  -0.373 0.086         0.764 241.133
spatial error  0.083 0.049  -0.534 0.128         0.793 242.401
spatial Durbin 0.060 0.051  -0.470 0.132         0.779 242.637
Code 
resid_I <- c(
  OLS = mr$estimate[[1]],
  lag = moran.test(residuals(sar), W)$estimate[[1]],
  error = moran.test(residuals(sem), W)$estimate[[1]]
)
round(resid_I, 3)
   OLS    lag  error 
 0.673 -0.018 -0.050
  • From OLS to the lag model the AIC falls by 190.6 points, with one more parameter. The residuals have no spatial pattern left (Moran’s I -0.02 and -0.05).
  • \(\rho\) = 0.76 and \(\lambda\) = 0.79: very strong dependence.
  • The strange result about the graduates is gone (for now: see section 7). The coefficient is 0.05 instead of 0.19, with a z of 1.5.
  • That of income is smaller: -0.37 (lag) and -0.53 (error). But the coefficients of the lag model are not effects, as section 6 shows.

Lag or error? The Lagrange multiplier tests

Code 
rs <- lm.RStests(ols, W, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"))
rs_tab <- t(sapply(rs, function(t) c(statistic = unname(t$statistic), p = unname(t$p.value))))
round(rs_tab, 4)
         statistic      p
RSerr     296.9890 0.0000
RSlag     284.3996 0.0000
adjRSerr   18.1518 0.0000
adjRSlag    5.5623 0.0184

Both simple tests are huge, because each also reacts to the other kind of dependence. The adjusted (robust) versions correct for this (Anselin et al., 1996). Here both are significant, the error version more clearly (18.2 against 5.6). The AICs of the two models are 241.1 and 242.4. The data do not decide between the two stories, and this is the usual outcome.

6. Effects in the lag model: direct and indirect

In the lag model a change of \(x\) in one region changes the unemployment of all regions, through \((I - \rho W)^{-1} = I + \rho W + \rho^2W^2 + \dots\). LeSage and Pace (2009) split the effect of \(x\) into

  • the direct effect: on the region itself, with the echo that comes back through the neighbours;
  • the indirect effect (spillover): on all the others together.
Code 
S <- solve(diag(n) - sar$rho * Wm)                              # (I - rho W)^-1
by_hand <- sapply(c("deg10", "log_gdp"), function(v) {
  M <- S * sar$coefficients[[v]]
  c(direct = mean(diag(M)), total = mean(rowSums(M)))
})
by_hand <- rbind(by_hand, indirect = by_hand["total", ] - by_hand["direct", ])
round(by_hand, 3)
         deg10 log_gdp
direct   0.060  -0.447
total    0.213  -1.582
indirect 0.153  -1.135
Code 
set.seed(141)
imp <- summary(impacts(sar, listw = W, R = 1000), zstats = TRUE, short = TRUE)
by_package <- sapply(imp$res[c("direct", "indirect", "total")], as.numeric)
rownames(by_package) <- c("deg10", "log_gdp")
round(by_package, 3)
        direct indirect  total
deg10    0.060    0.153  0.213
log_gdp -0.447   -1.135 -1.582
Code 
imp_ci <- t(sapply(
  c(direct = "direct_sum", indirect = "indirect_sum", total = "total_sum"),
  function(k) imp[[k]]$quantiles[2, c("2.5%", "97.5%")]
))
round(imp_ci, 2)
          2.5% 97.5%
direct   -0.63 -0.27
indirect -1.90 -0.70
total    -2.44 -1.02

The coefficient of log income is -0.37. The direct effect is -0.45, and the total -1.58, 95% CI [-2.44, -1.02]: if all the regions became 10% richer, unemployment would be 14.0% lower. Most of this, says the model, is spillover. But the split is a consequence of the formula: in a lag model the ratio of the indirect to the direct effect is the same for every predictor, whatever the data. It is a strong claim, and it rests on \(\rho\) being contagion.

7. What are the patches? Countries

Look again at the map. The edges of the patches are often national borders. Unemployment depends on the labour laws, the wages and the economy of the country. So give every country its own level:

Code 
ols_c <- lm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d)
mc    <- lm.morantest(ols_c, W)
sar_c <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d, listw = W)
sem_c <- errorsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp + factor(CNTR_CODE), data = d, listw = W)
comp <- rbind(
  `OLS` = c(coef(ols)[2:3], mr$estimate[[1]], AIC(ols)),
  `spatial lag` = c(sar$coefficients[2:3], resid_I[["lag"]], AIC(sar)),
  `OLS + countries` = c(coef(ols_c)[2:3], mc$estimate[[1]], AIC(ols_c)),
  `spatial lag + countries` = c(
    sar_c$coefficients[2:3],
    moran.test(residuals(sar_c), W)$estimate[[1]],
    AIC(sar_c)
  )
)
colnames(comp) <- c("deg10", "log_gdp", "Moran's I of the residuals", "AIC")
round(comp, 2)
                        deg10 log_gdp Moran's I of the residuals    AIC
OLS                      0.19   -0.92                       0.67 431.68
spatial lag              0.05   -0.37                      -0.02 241.13
OLS + countries          0.12   -0.84                       0.08 129.71
spatial lag + countries  0.10   -0.75                      -0.02 120.84
Code 
c(rho_without_countries = sar$rho, rho_with_countries = sar_c$rho)
rho_without_countries.rho    rho_with_countries.rho 
                0.7641573                 0.2410725

With country effects, plain OLS leaves a Moran’s I of 0.08, instead of 0.67. The \(\rho\) of the lag model falls from 0.76 to 0.24, and the AIC by another 111.4 points for the simple model with countries. Most of the “contagion” was the country. Within countries, unemployment falls with income (-0.84), and what is left of the neighbours is small. And the positive coefficient of the graduates is back (0.12, t = 2.4): the spatial models had hidden it. Within a country, regions with more graduates than their income suggests have a little more unemployment. The big cities may be part of it, but these data cannot say.

Code 
pairs <- data.frame(i = rep(seq_len(n), each = 5), j = unlist(W$neighbours))
pairs$same <- d$CNTR_CODE[pairs$i] == d$CNTR_CODE[pairs$j]
gap <- tapply(abs(d$log_u[pairs$i] - d$log_u[pairs$j]), pairs$same, mean)
gap
    FALSE      TRUE 
0.5555752 0.2816538
Code 
set.seed(142)
random_gap <- mean(abs(d$log_u - sample(d$log_u)))
random_gap
[1] 0.7494134

Neighbours in the same country differ by 0.28 on the log scale, neighbours across a border by 0.56, and two random regions by 0.75. The border explains a good part of the pattern, but not all of it: neighbours across a border are still more alike than strangers (compare Overman & Puga, 2002).

This is the general problem of spatial regression: a spatial lag absorbs whatever is missing and has a shape on the map. Gibbons and Overman (2012) gave their critique of the field the title “Mostly pointless spatial econometrics?” for this reason. A spatial model is a good way to get honest standard errors and to see that something is missing. It is a weak way to prove that things spread.

8. Does the definition of neighbours matter?

Code 
make_W <- list(
  `4 nearest` = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 4))),
  `5 nearest` = W,
  `8 nearest` = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 8))),
  `within 300 km` = nb2listw(dnearneigh(xy, 0, 300000), zero.policy = TRUE)
)
sens <- t(sapply(make_W, function(w) {
  m <- lagsarlm(log_u ~ deg10 + log_gdp, data = d, listw = w, zero.policy = TRUE)
  c(rho = m$rho, m$coefficients[2:3], AIC = AIC(m))
}))
round(sens, 3)
              rho.rho deg10 log_gdp     AIC
4 nearest       0.741 0.051  -0.361 247.229
5 nearest       0.764 0.050  -0.373 241.133
8 nearest       0.817 0.049  -0.351 239.145
within 300 km   0.706 0.105  -0.467 287.683

The definition changes the numbers (most of all with every region within 300 km) and not the story. Report more than one.

9. Things to keep in mind

  • Start with the map and Moran’s I of the residuals. If there is no pattern left, no spatial model is needed.
  • First add what is missing (countries, cities, coasts), then model what remains.
  • Lag for interaction, error for nuisance. Choose by theory. The tests rarely decide.
  • Never read the coefficients of a lag or Durbin model as effects. Use impacts.
  • \(W\) is chosen, not estimated. Say how, and try others.
  • Areas are arbitrary. Results can change with other borders or a finer division (the modifiable areal unit problem), and nothing follows for persons (the ecological fallacy, see beta regression).
  • Points instead of areas (sensors, houses): geostatistics, kriging (a Gaussian process on the map) or a smooth of the coordinates, mgcv::gam(y ~ x + s(lon, lat)).
  • Robust alternative: OLS with standard errors that allow for spatial correlation (Conley), if only the standard errors are the problem.

10. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the units, the weights matrix, Moran’s I before and after, the models and how they were chosen, impacts instead of coefficients for lag models, and the sensitivity to the weights. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("OLS", "Spatial lag", "Spatial error", "OLS with country effects"),
  deg = paste0(
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 1], coef(ols_c)[[2]])),
    " (",
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 2], coef(summary(ols_c))[2, 2])),
    ")"
  ),
  gdp = paste0(
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 3], coef(ols_c)[[3]])),
    " (",
    f2(c(tab[1:3, 4], coef(summary(ols_c))[3, 2])),
    ")"
  ),
  rho = c("—", f2(c(sar$rho, sem$lambda)), "—"),
  I = f2(c(mr$estimate[[1]], resid_I[["lag"]], resid_I[["error"]], mc$estimate[[1]])),
  AIC = f1(c(AIC(ols), AIC(sar), AIC(sem), AIC(ols_c)))
)

Method (data analysis):

We analysed the log unemployment rate (15–74 years, 2019) of 234 NUTS-2 regions of 31 European countries (Eurostat, 2024) with the share of adults with tertiary education and the log of GDP per head as predictors. Neighbours were the five nearest regions, with row-standardised weights. Spatial dependence was assessed with Moran’s I, and Lagrange multiplier tests (Anselin et al., 1996) compared a spatial lag and a spatial error model, estimated by maximum likelihood. For the lag model we report direct and total impacts (LeSage & Pace, 2009). Models with country effects and with other definitions of neighbours served as checks. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the packages spdep and spatialreg (Bivand & Piras, 2015).

Results:

Unemployment was strongly clustered, Moran’s I = 0.72, as were the residuals of the OLS model, I = 0.67, p < .001. Both spatial models fitted better (Table 1; ρ = 0.76, λ = 0.79), and the robust Lagrange multiplier tests did not clearly favour one of them (error: 18.2, lag: 5.6). In the lag model the total impact of log GDP was -1.58, 95% CI [-2.44, -1.02] (direct -0.45). With country effects, OLS left little spatial correlation in the residuals, I = 0.08, had a lower AIC than the spatial models, and gave a coefficient of -0.84 for log GDP: much of the spatial dependence is differences between countries.

Table 1

Regression Models of Log Unemployment in European Regions

Model Tertiary education (10 points) Log GDP per head ρ or λ Moran’s I of residuals AIC
OLS 0.19 (0.05) -0.92 (0.12) — 0.67 431.7
Spatial lag 0.05 (0.03) -0.37 (0.09) 0.76 -0.02 241.1
Spatial error 0.08 (0.05) -0.53 (0.13) 0.79 -0.05 242.4
OLS with country effects 0.12 (0.05) -0.84 (0.12) — 0.08 129.7

Note. N = 234. Coefficients with standard errors in parentheses. Coefficients of the spatial lag model are not marginal effects.

Points to remember:

  • Describe \(W\) exactly.
  • Report Moran’s I of the residuals of every model.
  • Report impacts for lag and Durbin models.
  • Say which story you assume, interaction or shared causes, and why.

11. Summary

When Observations have places, and neighbours resemble each other beyond the predictors
Detect Map, Moran’s I of the residuals
Lag model \(y = \rho Wy + X\beta + \varepsilon\): neighbours act on each other
Error model \(u = \lambda Wu + \varepsilon\): neighbours share what is missing
How (R) spdep::nb2listw(), spatialreg::lagsarlm(), errorsarlm(), impacts()
Reading it Lag: direct, indirect and total impacts. Error: ordinary coefficients
First Add the missing predictors (here: countries)
Report The weights, and what happens with others
Related pages Generalized least squares, beta regression, panel data

References

Anselin, L., Bera, A. K., Florax, R., & Yoon, M. J. (1996). Simple diagnostic tests for spatial dependence. Regional Science and Urban Economics, 26(1), 77–104. https://doi.org/10.1016/0166-0462(95)02111-6

Bivand, R., & Piras, G. (2015). Comparing implementations of estimation methods for spatial econometrics. Journal of Statistical Software, 63(18), 1–36. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v063.i18

Eurostat. (2024). Unemployment rates by NUTS 2 region [lfst_r_lfu3rt], population by educational attainment [edat_lfse_04], and GDP at current market prices by NUTS 2 region [nama_10r_2gdp] [Data sets]. https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/data/database

Gibbons, S., & Overman, H. G. (2012). Mostly pointless spatial econometrics? Journal of Regional Science, 52(2), 172–191. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9787.2012.00760.x

LeSage, J., & Pace, R. K. (2009). Introduction to spatial econometrics. CRC Press. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420064254

Overman, H. G., & Puga, D. (2002). Unemployment clusters across Europe’s regions and countries. Economic Policy, 17(34), 115–148. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0327.00085

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Time-Series Regression (ARIMAX): Did the Seat Belt Law Save Drivers?
item.description: Regression with ARIMA errors in R with arima() and the forecast package, on 16 years of monthly road casualties in Great Britain around the seat belt law of 1983: why least squares misjudges time series, seasonal differences, choosing the order with the ACF and AICc, the step effect of a law with petrol price and traffic as covariates, residual checks, the world without the law, placebo dates and a control group, spurious regression, and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Regression with ARIMA errors in R with arima() and the forecast package, on 16 years of monthly road casualties in Great Britain around the seat belt law of 1983: why least squares misjudges time series, seasonal differences, choosing the order with the ACF and AICc, the step effect of a law with petrol price and traffic as covariates, residual checks, the world without the law, placebo dates and a control group, spurious regression, and APA reporting.

The question: one law, one country, one date

On 31 January 1983 wearing a seat belt became compulsory for drivers and front-seat passengers in Great Britain. Did it save lives? The government asked two statisticians to find out (Harvey & Durbin, 1986).

There is no control group. The law came for everybody on the same day. All there is are the numbers of casualties, month by month, for years before and two years after. The question is whether the series stepped down at the date of the law, by more than its usual ups and downs.

A regression with a dummy variable for “after the law” seems to do it. But months that follow each other are not independent: a bad autumn affects several months, the economy goes in waves, and every December is worse than every June. Ordinary least squares takes neighbouring months for new information, and its standard errors are wrong.

Regression with ARIMA errors (often called ARIMAX) has two parts: a regression for what we want to know, and an ARIMA model for how the rest moves over time. Used for a question like this, it is called interrupted time series or intervention analysis (Box & Tiao, 1975).

Code 
library(forecast)   # Arima(), auto.arima(), forecast()
library(ggplot2)
# number formats for the text
f0   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
f1   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
f3   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")
# no leading zero
nz <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
pct  <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

1. The data

The data come with R, as the time series Seatbelts: 192 months, from January 1969 to December 1984.

Code 
head(Seatbelts, 2)
         DriversKilled drivers front rear  kms PetrolPrice VanKilled law
Jan 1969           107    1687   867  269 9059   0.1029718        12   0
Feb 1969            97    1508   825  265 7685   0.1023630         6   0
Code 
road <- data.frame(date = as.numeric(time(Seatbelts)), as.data.frame(Seatbelts))
y <- log(Seatbelts[, "drivers"]) # log of the car drivers killed or seriously injured
X <- cbind(
  law = Seatbelts[, "law"],
  petrol = log(Seatbelts[, "PetrolPrice"]),
  km = log(Seatbelts[, "kms"])
)
c(months = nrow(road), months_with_the_law = sum(road$law))
             months months_with_the_law 
                192                  23

drivers is the number of car drivers killed or seriously injured in the month, rear the same for rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern. kms is the distance driven, PetrolPrice the price of petrol, and law is 1 from February 1983. We take logarithms: effects on casualties are percentages, and a seasonal swing that grows with the level becomes constant.

2. Look at the data

Code 
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = road$date, n = road$drivers, who = "drivers"),
  data.frame(date = road$date, n = road$rear, who = "rear-seat passengers (no law)")
)
ggplot(long, aes(date, n)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1983 + 1 / 12, colour = "#eb6834", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~who, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Killed or seriously injured, per month",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: the seat belt law",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()
Code 
before <- mean(road$drivers[road$date >= 1982 & road$date < 1983])
after <- mean(road$drivers[road$date >= 1983 + 1 / 12 & road$date < 1984 + 1 / 12])
c(mean_1982 = before, mean_of_the_first_year = after, change = after / before - 1)
             mean_1982 mean_of_the_first_year                 change 
          1621.6666667           1277.9166667             -0.2119733

The drivers’ series has a strong yearly wave, a fall after the oil crisis of 1973–74, slow drifts, and a drop at the dashed line. In the year after the law there were 21% fewer casualties than in 1982. The series of the rear passengers shows no such drop. But how much of the drop is the law, and how much would have happened anyway?

3. Why least squares is not enough

Code 
month <- factor(cycle(y))
ols <- lm(y ~ X[, "law"] + X[, "petrol"] + X[, "km"] + month)
round(coef(summary(ols))[2:4, ], 3)
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
X[, "law"]      -0.161      0.023  -7.121    0.000
X[, "petrol"]   -0.403      0.057  -7.111    0.000
X[, "km"]       -0.157      0.046  -3.427    0.001
Code 
r_acf <- acf(resid(ols), plot = FALSE, lag.max = 24)$acf[-1]
round(r_acf[1:12], 2)
 [1] 0.45 0.38 0.26 0.20 0.27 0.21 0.18 0.09 0.16 0.10 0.20 0.20
Code 
lb_ols <- Box.test(resid(ols), lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box"); lb_ols$p.value
[1] 0

With a dummy for each month of the year, OLS finds an effect of the law of -0.16 on the log scale. But the residuals correlate with those of the next month at 0.45, and with those of two months later at 0.38. The Ljung–Box test of the first 24 autocorrelations has p < .001. The standard errors are too small, and they cannot be repaired by a formula that does not know how the series moves.

4. The model step by step, with formulas

Step 1: regression with errors that remember

\[y_t = \beta_1\,\text{law}_t + \beta_2\,\text{petrol}_t + \beta_3\,\text{km}_t + n_t\]

\(n_t\) is everything else, and it follows a time-series model. The \(\beta\)’s have their usual meaning.

Step 2: ARIMA, three ingredients

  • AR(p): today’s value depends on the last ones, \(n_t = \phi_1 n_{t-1} + \dots + e_t\).
  • MA(q): today’s value depends on the last shocks, \(n_t = e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \dots\).
  • I(d): the series is differenced \(d\) times to remove a drift, \(n_t - n_{t-1}\).

Step 3: the season

The same three for the same month of last year, with capital letters: ARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12}\). A seasonal difference (\(D = 1\)), \(n_t - n_{t-12}\), compares each month with the same month a year ago. It removes the yearly wave even if it changes slowly. When the errors are differenced, the regression is too: the law is compared as a change.

Step 4: what the estimate does

With AR(1) errors, the likelihood is that of the regression on quasi-differenced data, \(y_t - \phi y_{t-1}\) against \(x_t - \phi x_{t-1}\) (see generalized least squares). The new information of each month is only what the last month did not already say. By hand, for AR(1) errors and month dummies:

Code 
months <- model.matrix(~ month)[, -1]; Xm <- matrix(X, ncol = 3, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(X)))
Z  <- cbind(months, Xm); XX <- cbind(1, Z); n <- length(y)
profile_ll <- function(phi) {
  # exact likelihood for a given phi (Prais-Winsten)
  q <- function(v) c(sqrt(1 - phi^2) * v[1], v[-1] - phi * v[-n])
  f <- lm.fit(apply(XX, 2, q), q(as.numeric(y)))
  s2 <- mean(f$residuals^2)
  -n / 2 * (log(2 * pi * s2) + 1) + 0.5 * log(1 - phi^2)
}
phi_hat <- optimize(profile_ll, c(-0.99, 0.99), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
q <- function(v) c(sqrt(1 - phi_hat^2) * v[1], v[-1] - phi_hat * v[-n])
hand <- setNames(
  lm.fit(apply(XX, 2, q), q(as.numeric(y)))$coefficients,
  c("(Intercept)", colnames(Z))
)
ar1 <- arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = Z, method = "ML")
rbind(
  by_hand = c(phi = phi_hat, hand[c("law", "petrol", "km")]),
  arima = coef(ar1)[c("ar1", "law", "petrol", "km")]
)
             phi        law     petrol         km
by_hand 0.452686 -0.1731235 -0.3780838 -0.1324072
arima   0.452697 -0.1731300 -0.3780785 -0.1324141

5. Choosing the order

Code 
# searches over the orders, with the AICc
auto <- auto.arima(y, xreg = X, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
auto
Series: y 
Regression with ARIMA(1,0,3)(0,1,1)[12] errors 
Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1     ma2      ma3     sma1      law   petrol      km
      0.9818  -0.7106  0.0566  -0.1851  -0.8536  -0.2219  -0.3083  0.1077
s.e.  0.0184   0.0753  0.0982   0.0815   0.0789   0.0419   0.0946  0.1187
sigma^2 = 0.005586:  log likelihood = 208.25
AIC=-398.49   AICc=-397.43   BIC=-369.75
Code 
candidates <- list(
  `(1,0,0)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 0),
  `(1,0,1)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 1),
  `(2,0,1)(0,1,1)` = c(2, 0, 1),
  `(0,1,1)(0,1,1)` = c(0, 1, 1),
  `(1,0,3)(0,1,1)` = c(1, 0, 3)
)
fits <- lapply(candidates, function(o) Arima(y, order = o, seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), xreg = X))
comp <- t(sapply(fits, function(m) {
  c(
    AICc = m$aicc,
    law = coef(m)[["law"]],
    SE = sqrt(vcov(m)["law", "law"]),
    Ljung_Box_p = Box.test(resid(m), 24, fitdf = length(coef(m)) - 3, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value
  )
}))
round(comp, 3)
                   AICc    law    SE Ljung_Box_p
(1,0,0)(0,1,1) -381.611 -0.175 0.034       0.000
(1,0,1)(0,1,1) -395.050 -0.224 0.049       0.012
(2,0,1)(0,1,1) -395.573 -0.223 0.042       0.006
(0,1,1)(0,1,1) -389.272 -0.244 0.047       0.005
(1,0,3)(0,1,1) -397.432 -0.222 0.042       0.038

auto.arima() chooses the smallest AICc among many models. (AICs can only be compared between models with the same differences: the one with \(d = 1\) is in another league.) What matters more than the winner is the column law: whatever the order, the effect is between -0.24 and -0.18. The OLS estimate of -0.16 was smaller, probably because the month dummies and the straight regression could not follow the slow drifts. We take the winner.

Code 
fit <- auto
b <- coef(fit)[c("law", "petrol", "km")]; se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[c("law", "petrol", "km")]
tab <- cbind(b, SE = se, z = b / se, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(b / se)), effect = exp(b) - 1)
round(tab, 4)
             b     SE       z      p  effect
law    -0.2219 0.0419 -5.2909 0.0000 -0.1990
petrol -0.3083 0.0946 -3.2602 0.0011 -0.2653
km      0.1077 0.1187  0.9069 0.3645  0.1137
Code 
ci <- exp(b[["law"]] + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se[["law"]]) - 1
  • law = -0.222: the number of drivers killed or seriously injured was \(e^{-0.222}\) = 0.80 times what it would have been, a fall of 20%, 95% CI [13%, 26%].
  • petrol = -0.31: 10% higher petrol prices go with about 2.9% fewer casualties, with the distance held constant.
  • km is not clearly different from zero once the season and the memory are in the model.
  • The first coefficients (ar1, ma1, …, sma1) describe the memory. They are not effects, and nobody reports them one by one.

6. Checking the model

If the model is right, the residuals are white noise: no pattern left.

Code 
res <- data.frame(date = road$date, r = as.numeric(resid(fit)))[-(1:13), ]
a <- acf(res$r, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 24)
pa <- ggplot(res, aes(date, r)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2a78d6", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Residuals", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
pb <- ggplot(data.frame(lag = a$lag[-1], r = a$acf[-1]), aes(lag, r)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(res)),
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#eb6834"
  ) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Their autocorrelations", x = "lag (months)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
patchwork::wrap_plots(pa, pb, ncol = 1)
Code 
lb <- Box.test(resid(fit), lag = 24, fitdf = length(coef(fit)) - 3, type = "Ljung-Box")
c(Ljung_Box = lb$statistic, p = lb$p.value, Shapiro_p = shapiro.test(res$r)$p.value)
Ljung_Box.X-squared                   p           Shapiro_p 
        31.26106668          0.03778711          0.26997021

The Ljung–Box test has p = .038, so the residuals are not perfectly white: two or three autocorrelations at long lags (18 and 22 months) lie just outside the dashed limits, where one in twenty does by chance. Compared with the OLS residuals, nearly all of the memory is in the model. The other orders of the table do no better, and the effect of the law is nearly the same in all of them.

7. The world without the law

Fit the model to the months before the law only, and let it forecast the two years after, with the petrol prices and distances that really occurred:

Code 
last   <- c(1983, 1)
y_pre  <- window(y, end = last)
X_pre <- window(X[, c("petrol", "km")], end = last)
X_post <- window(X[, c("petrol", "km")], start = c(1983, 2))
pre    <- Arima(y_pre, order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3], seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6], xreg = X_pre)
fc     <- forecast(pre, xreg = X_post, level = 95)
post   <- subset(road, law == 1)
cf <- data.frame(
  date = post$date,
  observed = post$drivers,
  expected = exp(as.numeric(fc$mean)),
  low = exp(as.numeric(fc$lower)),
  high = exp(as.numeric(fc$upper))
)
saved  <- sum(cf$expected - cf$observed)
c(
  observed = sum(cf$observed),
  expected = sum(cf$expected),
  difference = saved,
  share = saved / sum(cf$expected)
)
    observed     expected   difference        share 
3.039900e+04 3.697005e+04 6.571046e+03 1.777397e-01

below
[1] 0.5652174

  geom_ribbon(

    inherit.aes = FALSE,

In the 23 months the forecast expected 36,970 casualties, and 30,399 happened: 6,571 fewer, or 18%. In 57% of the months the number was below the 95% band.

8. Attacks on the result

A control: the rear seats

If the fall came from better weather, better roads or less traffic, the rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern, would have profited too:

Code 
y_rear <- log(Seatbelts[, "rear"]); y_front <- log(Seatbelts[, "front"])
same_order <- function(v) {
  Arima(v, order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3], seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6], xreg = X)
}
rear  <- same_order(y_rear); front <- same_order(y_front)
eff <- function(m) {
  bb <- coef(m)[["law"]]
  s <- sqrt(vcov(m)["law", "law"])
  100 * c(effect = exp(bb) - 1, low = exp(bb - 1.96 * s) - 1, high = exp(bb + 1.96 * s) - 1)
}
controls <- rbind(
  drivers = eff(fit),
  `front-seat passengers` = eff(front),
  `rear-seat passengers` = eff(rear)
)
round(controls, 1)
                      effect   low  high
drivers                -19.9 -26.2 -13.0
front-seat passengers  -28.1 -34.6 -21.1
rear-seat passengers     2.5  -7.3  13.4

The effect in percent: drivers -20, front-seat passengers -28, rear-seat passengers 3, 95% CI [-7, 13]. Those whom the law did not concern saw no change that can be told from zero.

Placebo laws

Pretend that the law came at other dates, in the years before it existed, and estimate the “effect” each time:

Code 
dates <- seq(1971, 1981, by = 0.5)
placebo <- sapply(dates, function(d) {
  fake <- as.numeric(time(y_pre) >= d)
  m <- try(
    Arima(
      y_pre,
      order = arimaorder(fit)[1:3],
      seasonal = arimaorder(fit)[4:6],
      xreg = cbind(law = fake, X_pre)
    ),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  if (inherits(m, "try-error")) NA else coef(m)[["law"]]
})
pl <- data.frame(
  date = c(dates, 1983.08),
  b = c(placebo, b[["law"]]),
  kind = c(rep("invented dates", length(dates)), "the real law")
)
ggplot(pl, aes(date, 100 * (exp(b) - 1), fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey65", "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "The 'effect' of invented laws, and of the real one",
    x = NULL,
    y = "change of casualties (%)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Code 
larger <- sum(placebo <= b[["law"]], na.rm = TRUE)
c(placebos = sum(!is.na(placebo)), as_large_as_the_law = larger)
           placebos as_large_as_the_law 
                 21                   0

None of the invented dates should give much. A group of them does: those of the middle of the 1970s, after the oil crisis of the winter of 1973–74 had brought speed limits and empty roads. But 0 of the 21 invented dates gave a fall as large as the law’s. The method finds any step, whatever its cause. That the step of February 1983 is the law, and not something else that happened at the same time, is an argument from outside the model, and the rear seats are its best support.

9. Things to keep in mind

  • Two models share the name ARIMAX. Regression with ARIMA errors (here, and in arima(xreg = )) has coefficients with the usual meaning. Models with lags of \(y\) next to \(x\) (transfer functions) have not: there \(\beta\) is only the immediate effect.
  • Spurious regression. Two unrelated series that drift will correlate. Two random walks:
Code 
set.seed(131)
spur <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- cumsum(rnorm(100))
  b <- cumsum(rnorm(100))
  c(
    levels = summary(lm(a ~ b))$coefficients[2, 4] < .05,
    differences = summary(lm(diff(a) ~ diff(b)))$coefficients[2, 4] < .05
  )
})
rowMeans(spur)
     levels differences 
      0.752       0.050
  • OLS finds a “significant” relation between two independent random walks in 75% of the cases; after differencing, in 5%. With series that drift, difference or model the drift.
  • Shape of the effect. We assumed a sudden, permanent step. A law may work slowly, fade, or change the slope. Think first; a step is only the simplest shape.
  • Few points after the change make it hard to tell a step from the beginning of something else.
  • Anticipation. People may change before the date. Here many put on their belts in January 1983.
  • Covariates must not be changed by the intervention, and for forecasts their future values must be known.
  • Counts. These are large, so logs of them are fine. For small counts use time-series models for counts.
  • Structural models (level, slope and season that evolve) are the alternative that Harvey and Durbin used. They found a similar effect.

10. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) needs the series and its length, the transformation, the order of the ARIMA model and how it was chosen, the checks, the effect with its interval, and the evidence that it is the intervention. The numbers come from the R objects:

Code 
apa_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = c("Seat belt law", "Petrol price (log)", "Distance driven (log)"),
  b = f3(tab[, "b"]),
  SE = f3(tab[, "SE"]),
  z = f2(tab[, "z"]),
  p = sapply(tab[, "p"], function(p) sub("^= ", "", pval(p))),
  CI = paste0("[", f3(b - 1.96 * se), ", ", f3(b + 1.96 * se), "]")
)
order_text <- paste0(
  "ARIMA(",
  paste(arimaorder(fit)[1:3], collapse = ","),
  ")(",
  paste(arimaorder(fit)[4:6], collapse = ","),
  ")"
)

Method (data analysis):

The monthly number of car drivers killed or seriously injured in Great Britain, January 1969–December 1984 (192 months; Harvey & Durbin, 1986), was analysed on the log scale with a regression with ARIMA errors (interrupted time series; Schaffer et al., 2021). The seat belt law was coded as a step from February 1983; the log petrol price and the log distance driven were covariates. The order of the ARIMA model was chosen with the corrected AIC (Hyndman & Khandakar, 2008); residuals were checked with the Ljung–Box test. As controls we analysed front- and rear-seat passengers, invented dates before the law, and the forecast of the period after the law from the period before it. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the package forecast.

Results:

The selected model was ARIMA(1,0,3)(0,1,1)12; its residuals showed little autocorrelation, Ljung–Box Q(24) = 31.3, p = .038. The law was followed by a fall of 20% in the number of drivers killed or seriously injured, b = -0.222, SE = 0.042, 95% CI for the change [-26%, -13%] (Table 1). The forecast from the years before the law expected 6,571 more casualties in 23 months than were observed (18%). For rear-seat passengers, whom the law did not concern, the change was 3%, 95% CI [-7%, 13%].

Table 1

Regression With ARIMA Errors of the Log Number of Drivers Killed or Seriously Injured

Predictor b SE z p 95% CI
Seat belt law -0.222 0.042 -5.29 < .001 [-0.304, -0.140]
Petrol price (log) -0.308 0.095 -3.26 .001 [-0.494, -0.123]
Distance driven (log) 0.108 0.119 0.91 .364 [-0.125, 0.340]

Note. N = 192 months. Errors: ARIMA(1,0,3)(0,1,1)12. AICc = -397.4.

Points to remember:

  • Say what shape of effect was assumed (step, slope, pulse) and that it was chosen beforehand.
  • Report the order, the selection and the residual check, and how the effect changes with other orders.
  • Give the effect in percent, with an interval.
  • Show a control series or placebo dates.

11. Summary

When One long time series, predictors or an intervention, and errors that remember
The model \(y_t = x_t^\top\beta + n_t\), with \(n_t\) an ARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s\) process
How (R) forecast::auto.arima(y, xreg = X), or arima(y, order, seasonal, xreg)
Choosing AICc (same differences), then white-noise residuals
Reading it \(\beta\) as in any regression; on logs, \(e^\beta - 1\) is a percentage
Checks ACF of the residuals, Ljung–Box
For interventions Forecast without the intervention, control series, placebo dates
Danger Spurious regression of drifting series
Related pages Generalized least squares, panel data
